u1g9gw.text: Researchers warn that hackers could soon exploit a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-103849) affecting Magento and Adobe Commerce, potentially allowing them to execute arbitrary PHP code on store servers. According to e-commerce security firm Sansec, attacks leveraging the vulnerability, dubbed BlockStrap, have not yet been observed, but threat actors are expected to find a way to exploit it. The researchers based their assessment on identifying four potential attack paths involving CVE-2026-103849 in less than 24 hours. The flaw impacts September versions of Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source through 2.4.9 and Adobe Commerce B2B through 1.5.3. The security firm warned that Adobe’s “priority 2” rating of this flaw does not reflect the danger and urgency in this case, despite the more complex attack path. “The attack path is complex, but anyone with an AI agent can reverse-engineer the patch into working exploits in a relatively short time,” stated Sansec states. “That is why we question Adobe's priority 2 rating (patch within 30 days). StyleSmuggler went from a priority 1 hotfix to mass exploitation in three days, and BlockStrap is of similar complexity.” Adobe’s bulletin, published on October 13, describes the flaw as an improper neutralization of special elements used in a template engine, leading to arbitrary code execution. Sansec explains that BlockStrap is a second-pass template engine directive injection that allows attacker-controlled content in a child email template to be signed and processed again at the root level, executing a smuggled {{block}} directive. According to Sansec’s analysis, BlockStrap exposes a gap left by the StyleSmuggler fix in the same email-template engine. Adobe’s fix replaces the generic processing with registered placeholders, preventing exploitation. Sansec says that a plain Composer install isn’t enough to address the risk, and website administrators must apply the 2026-oct release or Adobe’s isolated patch. “BlockStrap and StyleSmuggler are separate fixes. You need both, so keep the September VULN-39341 hotfix in place as well,” Sansec cautions. The e-commerce security company says it will provide an update when it detects mass attack waves, which it expects to occur soon. 39bjr.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 16, 2026Vulnerability / OpenBSD A local privilege escalation exploit published today gains root on OpenBSD 7.9 by chaining a roughly 37-year-old integer overflow with a separate kernel flaw, bypassing OpenBSD's KARL kernel-address randomization and its SMAP and SMEP hardware protections. Security firm Calif, which found and reported the flaws, published a detailed writeup and full proof-of-concept code after OpenBSD shipped patches for both issues in September. The integer overflow in the shmat(4) attach function was fixed in errata 018, shipped September 14 as a reliability fix. The reference-counting use-after-free that completes the chain was fixed separately in errata 026, shipped September 30 as a security fix. Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures. OpenBSD 7.8 also received the integer-overflow fix. The integer overflow, the entry point for the full chain, is classified as a reliability fix, not a security fix. No CVE has been assigned for either flaw as of publication. There is no evidence that the vulnerabilities have been used in attacks. The shared-memory attachment counter shm_nattch is defined as a signed 16-bit short with a maximum value of 32,767 in original BSD sources dating to 1988. OpenBSD inherited the type and never widened it. The exploit maps 127 shared-memory segments and forks 259 processes, pushing the counter past its maximum and wrapping it to −32,643. A race condition then triggers a use-after-free: the corrupted reference count causes the kernel to free memory that other processes still use. A separate out-of-bounds write overwrites multicast-membership counters in the kernel. When the affected socket closes, the resulting decrements modify page-table entries, switching a user-memory mapping to supervisor-accessible and bypassing SMAP and SMEP. The exploit then overwrites a function pointer at a predictable kernel address to run its own code. "While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic," researcher Andrew Griffiths wrote. Both the boot-time and best-fit allocators lack base-address randomization, so early-boot structures, including function pointers in the lo0 and enc0 network-interface handlers, land at the same addresses across reboots on the same hardware. The exploit needs no information-disclosure vulnerability. Beyond the two errata, Calif proposes four categories of hardening: safe-unlinking for kernel linked lists (already used by FreeBSD and NetBSD), randomization of the page-table self-referential mapping, kernel-allocator randomization, and compiler-based bounds checking. Calif said it reported the flaws to OpenBSD "earlier this year." The proof-of-concept exploit code is available on GitHub.

hael9w.text: Candiru spyware was delivered to devices at Al Jazeera Media Network via targeted online advertisements in a zero-click attack that required only rendering the malicious ads on the victim's device. Researchers at Citizen Labs investigating the attacks referred to this technique as AdFection, noting that their report is the first public technical confirmation of mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. A similar method was documented in late 2025 by Amnesty International, involving ads that infected targets with Predator spyware without them clicking anything. That infection mechanism was called Aladdin and surfaced due to a collection of marketing files and documents leaked from the Intellexa surveillance company that researchers studied and corroborated with technical details from forensic investigations. Unlike Alladin, AdFection was caught in real attacks and linked to Israeli firm Discovere-Tech, described by Citizen Lab as " a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem." Ads participating in AdFectionSource: Citizen Lab Zero-click Candiru spyware infection According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech allowed its customers to use its Controlium platform to target specific devices with malicious code, or profile, deanonimize, and fingerprint user devices. "Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem," Citizen Lab says. The company purchased ad placements through mainstream ad networks and exchanges, embedding JavaScript in ads that contacted its "NOAS server" when rendered. Using multiple parameters (e.g., IP address, ad identifiers), the NOAS server, "or getAd server," determined if a target was eligible to receive JavaScript code. Selected targets received additional code, while other devices the ad rendered on received nothing, helping keep the attacks stealthy. Action sequence for valid targetsSource: Citizen Lab Al Jazeera provided Citizen Lab with evidence of attacks that targeted at least 45 devices between 2024 and 2025. The network logs examined by the researchers showed a sequence from Discover-Tech infrastructure to Candiru validation servers and then to spyware command-and-control servers. The researchers also recovered a DLL file from a compromised Windows system and attributed it with high confidence to Candiru, based on infrastructure and code overlaps with previously captured samples. Candiru is an Israeli spyware vendor that sells surveillance tools, officially only to governments. The company also developed malware for Windows called DevilsTongue, which can steal files, credentials, and messages. According to past reports, its tools have been deployed through Windows and Chrome zero-day exploits against journalists, activists, politicians, and other targets. Candiru attack chainSource: Citizen Lab While Al Jazeera is one confirmed target of these attacks, Citizen Lab reports that the advertising operation placed 3.77 billion bids and won 442 million auctions between March and June 2026. Ads assessed to carry attacker script tags appeared across 75,373 Android/iOS apps and 120,768 websites, although these figures do not represent infection counts. “We estimate that between hundreds of thousands and millions of users were directed to these domains via Discover-Tech ads,” explains Citizen Lab. After receiving Citizen Lab's reports, major advertising companies like Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Eskimi, and Vungle took action to remove offending accounts and block access to domains. oyxhl2.text: Attackers repeatedly changed the files that AOMEI Backupper fetches from the vendor's own update servers, in windows of five to ten minutes at a time between May and July 2026, so that any copy of the Windows backup program that checked for an update during one of those windows would download and run a backdoor. Google Threat Intelligence Group, Mandiant, and ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab, which disclosed the campaign this week, say AOMEI has reported fixing its servers, but that fix does not remove the backdoor from machines that were already hit. AOMEI Backupper is Windows backup and disk-cloning software made by AOMEI Technology, a vendor registered in Hong Kong. Like the company's remote-desktop tool AnyViewer, it runs background services that regularly check AOMEI's servers over HTTPS for software updates and promotional pop-ups. Two files drive that check. One, down_html.ini, names the update package to download and the checksum the program uses to verify it. The other, Notifycfg.ini, tells the pop-up service what to display and what to run. The program does not cryptographically verify either file, and the checksum that is supposed to prove the download is genuine sits inside the same unsigned file that names it. Nothing in the software was exploited. There was no vulnerability, and no user action was needed beyond having the program installed and running, according to ManageEngine's lab. The attacker only had to change two text files on the server for a few minutes. A copy of Backupper that checked in during a window pulled the attacker's package into its own folder, and the notification file then made it run. It ran with the privileges of the AOMEI process that launched it. On the machines the lab examined, that was enough to install software across the whole system, though it said the elevation depended on how the AOMEI service was running. Three Windows, Eleven Countries GTIG and Mandiant confirmed three tampering windows, and said more probably happened that they did not see: May 28, 2026: a 10-minute window, 05:40 to 05:50 UTC July 16, 2026: a 6-minute window, 08:33 to 08:39 UTC July 20, 2026: a 5-minute window, 10:35 to 10:40 UTC Only copies that checked for an update during a window were affected. A copy that checked before or after got clean, genuine files, which is what makes the attack hard to catch. GTIG described the targeting as opportunistic, hitting whatever system happened to poll during those minutes. From its own telemetry, GTIG identified affected organizations in IT services, telecommunications and higher education across 11 countries: Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye and the United States. It gave no total and said the real number is likely higher. GTIG named AnyViewer, AOMEI's remote-desktop tool, as using the same update flow, but the detections it describes involve Backupper. Neither report lists which Backupper versions are affected, and the lab examined version 8.3.0. GTIG tracks the group behind the campaign as UNC7017 and names no country or known actor. It said this is the first supply chain compromise it has encountered built on Windows this short, "effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning." What Landed on the Machine On a machine that pulled the package, a downloader that GTIG calls CROSSROAD unpacked a bundle into a local Radmin folder, created a scheduled task set to run every three hours, and then deleted itself from disk. The bundle included a genuine, signed copy of Radmin, a commercial remote-administration tool. ManageEngine's lab found it staged but never switched on, with no listener, no configuration, and no new account. The remote control came instead from a separate implant that reached out to the attacker. The scheduled task runs the signed Radmin program, which loads an attacker-built DLL placed beside it, which in turn loads the SHINYROAD implant. The implant gives a remote shell and can fetch and run new code on command. It talks to a single hard-coded address with no backup, so blocking that one address cuts off the attacker's control. CROSSROAD runs only in some places. It checks the machine's location and stops if it is in China, and ManageEngine added that it also stops if it finds particular security agents on the host. On machines that passed those checks, GTIG later saw a second tool pushed down on top of SHINYROAD, the open-source Adaptix C2 framework, disguised as Nitro PDF software. A July 20 Change That Needed No Code to Run The July 20 window included a second trick that did not require running any program. GTIG found that the notification file had been changed to open an invisible, one-pixel pop-up pointing to a file on an attacker's server via WebDAV, a way to access a remote file as if it were on the local disk. Rendering that pop-up can make Windows send the logged-in user's NetNTLMv2 authentication response, a token an attacker can try to crack offline or reuse, to the attacker's address with nothing visible to the user. Because no program had to run, a machine with the backdoor blocked could still have leaked that token. What AOMEI Was Told, and When ManageEngine's lab said its endpoint software first caught the activity on May 28, when it recorded AOMEI Backupper installing Radmin on two unrelated customers in different countries. A customer raised it on June 7, and the lab notified AOMEI the same day. AOMEI's first explanation was that the content had been intercepted and changed in transit. The lab said the evidence did not support that explanation. Both machines had fetched the files over HTTPS from AOMEI's own servers, across different countries and networks, and the program had pulled the package in through its normal update steps. In mid-July, its own monitors caught one of the windows as it happened, confirming the change was being served from AOMEI's side. Mandiant notified AOMEI on July 17 and shared indicators. AOMEI told Mandiant on July 29 that it had taken corrective action to secure its servers. ManageEngine's lab said that, as of publication, it had not independently confirmed that the compromise had been contained. Neither report says how the attacker gained the ability to change files on AOMEI's servers. AOMEI's published changelog for Backupper, checked by The Hacker News on October 16, lists no change to how the program verifies updates through the current release, 8.5.0, from October 9. Neither report points to a version that closes the gap. What to Check Now A fixed server does not clean a machine that was hit. The downloader set up its scheduled task and then restored the local update file to its genuine contents, so an infected machine can look normal while the vendor's download page also looks clean. GTIG and ManageEngine both urge organizations running AOMEI software to hunt across the whole April-to-July period. "Organizations running AOMEI software cannot assume they are protected solely because the vendor took corrective server-side action," GTIG and Mandiant said. Do not judge an alert by checking the vendor's download page now. Because the files changed back within minutes, that page serves genuine content almost all the time, which has led analysts to dismiss real detections as false alarms. Preserve the files cached in the program's own folders, and check network logs for what was served at the exact time the alert fired. On the endpoint, hunt for: Scheduled task: RadminComponentRuntime, or NitroRuntime for the follow-on tool File: an unsigned upgrade-now.exe that carries AOMEI's publisher details, or any program running from Backupper's html pop-up folder Folder: attacker files staged under the local Radmin application-data folder On the network, block the attacker infrastructure named in both reports, and block outbound SMB (TCP 445) and WebDAV to external addresses to stop the credential trick: Domain: storage-data[.]com, promotion.storage-data[.]com, aomei.storage-data[.]com IP: 8.210.84[.]56, 8.218.65[.]184, 47.239.60[.]117 GTIG and ManageEngine each published detection rules with their reports, YARA rules from GTIG and Sigma rules from the lab. Both sets are the researchers' own and have not been tested by The Hacker News.

vrjppe.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 16, 2026Phishing / Artificial Intelligence Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an advanced persistent threat (APT) spear-phishing campaign that has targeted individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations to direct victims to an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing framework designed to harvest their Google account credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes. The activity is being tracked by Cisco Talos under the moniker UAT-11985, describing it as likely fueled by artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted content generation so as to quickly craft bespoke lures aimed at different targets within the confines of a common social engineering framework. The campaign was first observed in mid-2026. "The operation leveraged legitimate public event themes and impersonated reputable academic and policy institutions to establish credibility," Talos researcher Joey Chen said in an analysis. "Beyond traditional email phishing, the actor incorporated QR code phishing (quishing) techniques by modifying legitimate event posters with malicious QR codes, expanding the attack surface beyond email recipients to secondary victims who may encounter printed materials." Central to the operation is the use of legitimate or plausible public event information in spear-phishing emails and embedding within them a URL that points to attacker-controlled infrastructure, while hovering over the hyperlink displays a legitimate-looking Google Forms URL. These invitation emails feature nearly identical syntactic structures despite the breadth of geopolitical topics being discussed, indicating the content was mass-produced from a reusable prompt template rather than painstakingly crafted for each target. Specifically, the emails follow a three-part structure - The opening section offers a "polished (but overly elaborate) description" of the geopolitical or policy context. The second section is tailored to the recipient and paints them in a flattering light in an attempt to trigger engagement. The third and final section provides details of event logistics, including the topic, date, venue, and registration instructions. The threat actor has been found to impersonate legitimate Taiwan-based institutions like the Taiwan European Union Centre, NCCU Institute of International Relations, and Taiwan Research Institute, fabricating the sender identities to make the messages appear more convincing. "Taken together, the reuse of an almost-identical narrative structure, rhetorical style, personalized flattery, institutional impersonation, and deceptive registration mechanism strongly suggests a coordinated and carefully targeted spear-phishing campaign rather than three independent invitations," Talos said. In a subset of cases, the phishing emails incorporate legitimate event posters scraped from legitimate websites, but with the QR codes modified to trick victims into scanning the malicious QR code to "register" for the event. The phishing site imitates the look of a legitimate Google Form, but the primary goal of the site is to serve a pop-up that prompts the victim to sign-in with their Google account to complete the form. Doing so takes them to a bogus site featuring a spoofed Google login panel to capture their credentials and authentication challenges. The pixel-perfect replica site is an adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) proxy that uses obfuscated JavaScript to gather and exfiltrate the entered information in real-time over a WebSocket connection, while simultaneously forwarding it to legitimate Google authentication servers. Prior to establishing the WebSocket connection, the JavaScript payload collects device and browser information, including the locale, user agent, screen dimensions, and mobile-device status, which are then reported to the command-and-control (C2) server via a "google_login_start" request. When the victim submits the password, the phishing page transmits the password, along with the account identifier and browser user-agent information, to the actor's HTTP C2 server through a "google_login_check" request. The threat actor's server, placed in an AitM position, then forwards the credentials to the actual Google authentication service. "The spoofed Google login panels only support Simplified Chinese (zh-CN), Traditional Chinese (zh-TW), and English locales, with region detection based on the victim's browser 'navigator.languages,' strongly suggesting targeting of Chinese-speaking users," Chen explained. "By deliberately splitting one-shot uploads with POST requests from low-latency state updates with WebSocket connection, the threat actor has engineered a seamless credential-harvesting relay. This allows the threat actor to mirror Google's dynamic authentication state in real time, ultimately achieving full account takeover without raising the victim's suspicion."

pvfw4c.text: Cybersecurity giant Proofpoint says it will acquire a similarly long-running company, Varonis, in an all-cash transaction worth $6.3 billion. “The combined company will serve more than 16,000 enterprises and millions of organizations globally, creating one of the world’s leading pure-play cybersecurity companies and establishing the industry's largest data and AI cybersecurity organization,” Proofpoint said in announcing the deal on Thursday. Miami-based Varonis, founded in 2005, focuses on data visibility and security. The footprint for California-headquartered Proofpoint, founded in 2002, traditionally includes email security and identity threat defense. AI figured prominently in Thursday’s announcement. The goal is to create a platform that “helps organizations adopt AI with confidence: finding and protecting sensitive data, controlling what people and AI can access, and stopping data loss.” Both companies are known for their cybersecurity research. Varonis researchers recently got headlines for a report in which they manipulated Microsoft’s AI assistant Copilot Personal into explaining how to hack itself. Proofpoint analysts published research earlier this month about a high-level, apparently China-backed phishing campaign geared toward espionage.

fabr8i.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 16, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Web Security OpenAI has disclosed seven new incidents in which its artificial intelligence (AI) models exhibited misaligned behavior, including one case where its research model, after not having funds on an Ethereum test network, spent test cryptocurrency from a third-party's wallet without authorization to complete a coding task. The incident, the AI company said, involved an internal research model part of the GPT-5.6 Sol family. The incident occurred on June 26, 2026, and was discovered by OpenAI three months later. "An internal research model asked to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a wallet that the task had not supplied to pay for a deployment on Sepolia, an Ethereum test network," OpenAI said. "It derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment." The assignment allowed the model to deploy compatible contracts if it did not find one, but gave it no funded wallet to pay the network fees. After its attempts to obtain free test tokens failed, it wrote a script to derive "accounts from common developer recovery phrases and query their balances." In the process, it identified 362 addresses and found one account that held enough Sepolia ETH. Armed with the recovery (or seed) phrase, the model derived the private keys that grant unauthorized access to the corresponding account and spend the stashed cryptocurrency. Although the model questioned whether it had the necessary permission to carry out this step, it subsequently reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. "But using public known key/funds ethically? Funds on a known public dev mnemonic are effectively abandoned/test ETH; Sepolia valueless," the model mused. "We can use [amount redacted] to deploy task. Fine." OpenAI has since implemented additional safeguards to prevent live internet access for such scenarios, adding it runs its misalignment monitoring system on all traffic to flag events if its AI agents manage to gain live internet access. "This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI said. Besides using a funded test cryptocurrency wallet without authorization, OpenAI said it identified six more cases of misalignment involving its models, adding to three other incidents it revealed at the start of this month - June 16, 2026, when an internal research model bypassed a restriction limiting internet access to HTTP GET requests as part of efforts to seek public trade statistics. It achieved this by using an external browser to send requests on its behalf, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. June 16 and 17, 2026, when an internal model developed and tested ways to bypass restrictions on internet access during reinforcement learning and explored ways to contact outside services, and continued testing these approaches even after obtaining the statistics it was seeking, such as teacher salaries in Merrowen, connections to the electrical grid in Orvessa, and disability counts in Bellora. June 17, 2026, when a highly persistent internal model tasked with retrieving figures from a public research dashboard accessed an unspecified organization's internal systems and changed their configuration. The model altered a setting to obtain a cloud-storage access token and downloaded non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. Not only did the model not disclose these actions, it restored the modified setting, but continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. June 17, 2026, when a highly persistent internal model deployed as part of a data-retrieval task in reinforcement-learning training abused a government statistics website's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials. It then analyzed the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, retrieved data that it was denied access to, and stored it locally. The data included annual statistics spanning 24 years, including years beyond the requested year. In its answer, the model made no mention of the fact that it had obtained unauthorized access. June 19 and 20, 2026, when its internal research models bypassed restrictions on internet access to allow only HTTP GET requests to fetch figures from government entities' public data sources by writing custom programs to send a POST request through a custom network connection. October 6, 2026, when an internal research model assigned to grade seven responses attempted to submit unsupported assessments after it found that the required input files were missing. When the automated check rejected its bogus grading report, the model tried to create fake input files in an attempt to pass the checks. After this also resulted in failure, the model took the step of damaging its task environment in hopes of triggering a reset. "In response to this and other incidents, we hardened our security controls, took additional steps to prevent models from accessing the live internet during training, improved alignment grading, and extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic," OpenAI said.

1bknwo.text: Article written by Vakaris Noreika, VP of Product Research and Development at NordLayer Monday morning, you handle security for an organization, and suddenly, your security tools flag personal ChatGPT use on a managed laptop, even though your org pays for ChatGPT Enterprise. You wonder what the employee submitted to ChatGPT. Could be a public job description, or a customer ticket with contact information and internal account details. Maybe sensitive government documents, if that is your line of work, as the acting director of CISA did in 2025? The case is hypothetical. In this article, we will follow 2 versions of the same event. In the first, your security tools identify personal account use, but nothing in your current configuration checks what goes into the prompt. In the second, NordLayer AI Scout is deployed on the managed browser, with a custom detector set to “Block” for your customer account number format. What do you do next? 1. Confirm the account and the employee You start with the basics. With only your existing controls, you open the event that flagged personal ChatGPT use and work out which identity belongs to what. The user who signed in to your security tools may have a corporate email address. But the ChatGPT login behind the event may be a personal Gmail account. That gives you 1 person, 2 identities, and 1 awkward conversation ahead. With NordLayer AI Scout, the signed-in ChatGPT account appears beside the conversation, and the tool classifies new ChatGPT conversations as Personal or Corporate. Activity is tied to a person through the work email that your MDM tool pushes to the device. Directory sync with Entra ID, Okta, or HiBob adds the department, team, and role information. 2. Establish what reached ChatGPT In the first scenario, the retained event says the employee used a personal account. It holds no prompt text and no sensitive data findings, so you can’t rebuild the submission from it. Under the incident review procedure, you ask the employee to show you the conversation. Better keep the request narrow and limit it to the work exchange around that timestamp, unless you want a tour of your colleague’s meal plans or medical questions. Let’s say, the customer ticket is right there in the prompt, and ChatGPT's reply discusses it in detail. You now have evidence that customer information reached the service. With NordLayer AI Scout, you open the blocked finding. The browser extension had checked the prompt on the device before it left. A configured detector matched the customer data, and the “Block” action stopped the submission. The employee then saw an on-page notice that the prompt had been blocked. Nobody on the security team needed to read the prompt for this to happen. See AI use beyond the approved tool list Get a clearer picture of how employees use AI tools and coding agents across your organization, including applications that may be operating outside your approved tool list. Try NordLayer AI Scout for 30 days and put that visibility to work. Start Free Trial 3. Ask why the corporate access went unused There’s a 99% chance that the explanation is mundane: the corporate session had expired, 2FA took too long, the customer was upset, and the personal ChatGPT tab was already open and signed in. The employee says that’s why they pasted a customer support exchange into the chat, typed “Draft a response explaining why this customer cannot access their account,” and pressed “Send.” Without a matching prompt-blocking rule, the prompt reached ChatGPT. Good. Next, you should find out whether this was the first time. Without NordLayer AI Scout in place, you depend on the employee’s memory. You have to ask whether they ever pasted whole tickets before, uploaded attachments, or created shared conversation links, and generally whether personal ChatGPT became their plan B every time the corporate session expired. It is also a good idea to ask what they understood about the policy. Sometimes people remember that ChatGPT is approved, but they forget which workspace and data it applies to. 4. Respond to the outcome you confirmed Without dedicated prompt-level controls, customer data reached a completed conversation in a personal ChatGPT account. You should preserve the evidence you need and bring in the incident, privacy, or data owner. Then, judge how serious it is based on what was shared. If credentials were exposed, they need revocation or rotation. If it’s customer records, the process may need a privacy assessment. If public text was pasted, there’s no data incident at all, but it makes sense to have a word with the employee about their more powerful Enterprise seat, which is paid for. In any case, you should keep the write-up accurate, because using a personal account does not prove that the prompt went into model training, became public, or reached another user. You confirmed that company data entered a service through an account outside of the approved arrangement—that is serious enough without embellishment. If you use NordLayer AI Scout, you just record that the configured rule blocked this submission. The event shows an attempted policy violation and the control that stopped it. If the employee mentions earlier use of their personal account, you assess it separately. 5. Fix the workflow before you close the ticket You help with the 2FA and ask the employee to sign in to the Enterprise workspace and finish the support task there so you can see it work. However, an Enterprise subscription does not mean that employees can submit anything, so you also verify that the task and data are permitted. In the first scenario, you review restrictions on personal instances and the DLP rules that apply. With NordLayer AI Scout, you confirm the prompt policy on the browser extension. “Warn,” “Redact,” and “Block” do different jobs. “Warn” pauses the send and lets the employee choose whether to send anyway or go back and edit the text. “Redact” removes the matched value and sends the rest. “Block” stops the prompt. You pick the action that fits each data category. Then, you document the account, the device, the confirmed contents, whether the prompt was sent, and who owns the response. Finally, you record the access fix and schedule a check for repeat events. All in all, in one version, customer data reached personal ChatGPT and needed an exposure assessment. In the other, the configured detector blocked the prompt before it left the device. In both versions, the employee needs corporate access that works on a Monday morning. Without it, the ticket will close, and a workaround will be ready by tomorrow. About the author: Vakaris Noreika, VP of Product Research and Development, is a cybersecurity expert who oversees the development of business security products at NordLayer, a toggle-ready network security platform for businesses. He has many years of experience working on threat intelligence, network security, data privacy, and automated monitoring. He focuses on controls that reduce exposure without creating unnecessary operational overhead. Sponsored and written by NordLayer AI Scout.

9q9c3k.text: Russian authorities have reportedly detained three suspected members of the DataSuckers hacking group following a cyberattack on a popular restaurant chain that exposed vast amounts of customer information. A Moscow court on Wednesday placed 19-year-old Denis Fridman under house arrest until December 8 in connection with the Dodo Pizza breach, which reportedly involved the theft of records related to hundreds of millions of orders placed over 15 years. He faces charges connected to the illegal handling of computer information containing personal data. Fridman is one of four alleged members of DataSuckers, a financially motivated hacking group that has claimed responsibility for recent attacks on major businesses in Russia and Ukraine. Two other suspects have been detained while a fourth remains at large, according to Russian newspaper Kommersant and Telegram news outlet Baza. The suspects reportedly include citizens of Russia, Kazakhstan and Belarus. According to Baza, police identified the suspected hackers after Fridman accidentally exposed his IP address while accessing data stolen from Dodo Pizza, allowing authorities to trace him to his home in the Russian city of Barnaul. The attack reportedly began when the hackers discovered Dodo Pizza's corporate credentials exposed on GitHub. Using those credentials, the attackers allegedly gained access to interconnected company systems, including cloud storage and databases, as well as stored passwords. Kommersant reported that the stolen database was offered for sale on the dark web and that the hackers received $100,000 for the archive, with the money transferred to a shared cryptocurrency wallet. The wallet's password was reportedly changed after Fridman's arrest. Recorded Future News could not independently verify the circumstances that led Russian law enforcement to the suspects. Dodo Pizza, a Russian fast-food chain operating approximately 1,500 restaurants across 28 countries, previously acknowledged that attackers may have accessed customer information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth and order details. Attacks across Russia and Ukraine DataSuckers has emerged in recent months, claiming responsibility for attacks on major businesses in Russia and Ukraine. In September, the group claimed responsibility for breaching Russian tour operator Tez Tour, saying it had spent about two weeks inside the company's systems and obtained large amounts of customer information. The hackers also defaced the company's website. Tez Tour acknowledged the disruption but disputed claims that customer data had been compromised, saying it had isolated its internal systems before the attackers could access them. Fridman allegedly participated in that attack, according to Kommersant. The newspaper reported that he had previously targeted Ukrainian websites before joining DataSuckers. Earlier this month, the group claimed responsibility for an attack on ATB, Ukraine's largest grocery store chain, demanding $400,000 and threatening to publish data it claimed to have stolen from millions of customers. The hackers placed an extortion message and a countdown timer on the retailer's website, which subsequently became unavailable. ATB denied that customer information had been compromised and said it had temporarily taken some online services offline for technical maintenance. DataSuckers claimed to have obtained records belonging to 7.9 million ATB customers, including names, contact information, addresses and password hashes, as well as employee passport information and more than 11 million order records. Those claims have not been independently verified. The group describes itself as financially motivated rather than politically aligned. It primarily communicates in Russian and uses a public Telegram channel to announce attacks, publish details of alleged intrusions and invite victims, journalists and law enforcement agencies to contact its members. In a message posted last weekend, DataSuckers said it was continuing operations but would reduce its public activity. "We're operating as usual, but you'll be seeing less public activity from us," the group said. "For now, we're focused on specific targets and working on them." The group has not published any further messages on its Telegram channel since that statement. 5vtblu.text: Officials in Anne Arundel County, Maryland, confirmed that hackers stole files from government systems during an incident in August. A county spokesperson told Recorded Future News that they discovered “irregular activity” on August 28 and began an investigation on a “limited subset of systems within the county computer network.” “Through the course of the county’s response and investigation, it was determined that an unauthorized actor gained access to a limited number of systems and copied certain files from those systems,” the spokesperson said. The spokesperson did not respond to questions about what data was involved but said investigators are currently reviewing the files to determine whether any stolen information related to residents of the county. The Baltimore suburb is home to more than 600,000 residents and the state’s capital of Annapolis. Washington, D.C. is nearby, as well. Dozens of federal agencies have offices or headquarters in the county, including the Defense Department, the Internal Revenue Service, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Social Security Administration, the Department of Agriculture, the U.S. Coast Guard and more. County officials said they notified federal law enforcement about the data breach as well as other government agencies. The attack was claimed by the Rhysida ransomware gang, which threatened to leak 2.6 terabytes worth of documents stolen from the county if a $2 million ransom was not paid. The group recently attempted to extort the government of Berlin after stealing troves of emails and contracts from government systems. Rhysida has repeatedly targeted governments across the globe since emerging several years ago. Its victims include Kuwait’s Finance Ministry, the city of Seattle and the city of Columbus, Ohio and even the transportation department of Maryland. Anne Arundel County dealt with a ransomware attack by a different group last year that forced the government to shut off multiple systems. In a stroke of bad luck, the county released a new statement about last year’s attack on Thursday evening, telling residents that it planned to send out breach notification letters about leaked data in that incident on October 19. A spokesperson for the county told Recorded Future News that the August 28 attack is a “separate incident.” The Anne Arundel County spokesperson added that recent reports “indicate that there has been a surge in these kinds of calculated cybercrimes specifically targeting state and local governments.” Cities and counties in New Mexico, Utah, Texas, Nebraska, Missouri and Arizona have all dealt with service outages over the last two weeks due to cyberattacks. qodeh3.text: An alleged Chinese state-backed group is using a new zero-day in BeyondTrust software to conduct espionage attacks. BeyondTrust, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed the zero-day on Thursday evening, publishing incident reports detailing attacks involving the bug. The identity security company said the vulnerability affects its Remote Support appliances that enable IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. A patch has been released addressing the issue and several mitigations are available. Other cybersecurity firms have since confirmed exploitation. The company said it was first tipped off to the bug — tagged as CVE-2026-102764 — on September 27, when an attack against another vendor's edge appliances became public and sparked an investigation into a similar issue. Mandiant also warned BeyondTrust of a potential vulnerability, sending the company’s engineering team on a hunt that led them back to a zero-day exploited on August 29. Mandiant incident responders said the attackers were able to escalate their privileges after exploiting the bug, moving laterally within the victim’s network and establishing a deeper foothold. They noted that the group behind the attacks — which they call Armory Castle or UNC5221 — “leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals” due to their abuse of proprietary tools. Mandiant saw the group use custom malware they call Sawfly and Bareclaw. The threat actors found a way to get every credential the appliance stored and were able to modify files that survive reboots and configuration resets. Mandiant warned that any vulnerable appliance that was reachable from the internet should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. ‘Long-term intelligence collection’ BeyondTrust confirmed Mandiant’s assessment that Armory Castle is a Chinese “state-sponsored espionage operation focused on long-term intelligence collection.” “ARMORY CASTLE’s documented targets include legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology companies, and government,” the company said, noting that researchers believe the group targets technology firms to help with the discovery of other zero-day exploits. The group was previously responsible for exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in popular edge devices and was known to use passive backdoors and other novel tools to sustain their access to breached systems. The group has been active since October 2023 and Google said they have “targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations.” “In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed,” they said. “It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764.” Google compared the situation to previous incidents where the same threat actors conducted widespread exploitation of two bugs affecting products from IT firm Ivanti following their disclosure. Armory Castle was also previously implicated in exploiting zero-days affecting Citrix as well as multiple issues in Ivanti products, including CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, and CVE-2025-0282. “In 2025, Mandiant reported that the actor took an Ivanti patch for a flaw that had been rated low risk, studied it, and turned it into working remote code execution against unpatched appliances,” BeyondTrust said. “The actor uses a zero-day selectively against chosen targets, and once the vulnerability is public, the actor typically moves to broad exploitation of every instance still unpatched.” Last year, Mandiant and multiple U.S. agencies warned about activity from the group targeting governments, legal firms, software-as-a-service providers and technology companies. 1jmywh1.text: Burger King Japan, the Japanese subsidiary of global fast-food giant Burger King, disclosed a major data breach after attackers accessed a server containing 11.18 million customer records. Founded in 1953 in Florida, Burger King is now a multinational fast-food chain with nearly 20,000 locations worldwide, including 350 in Japan. In a Thursday press release, Burger King Japan said it concluded a follow-up investigation on October 13 and apologized to customers whose data was stolen in early October and leaked online. The breached servers stored the personal information for users of the company's official smartphone app, including their names, dates of birth, gender, email addresses, phone numbers, and order history. "We identified a potential unauthorized third-party access to the system that manages member information for our official app and conducted an investigation," Burger King Japan said. "As a result, it was determined on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, that unauthorized access occurred between Friday, October 2, 2026, and Wednesday, October 7, 2026, resulting in a leak of member information. Upon becoming aware of the unauthorized access, we immediately blocked access from the source in question." However, the company says the compromised server did not store customer credit card numbers and that it found no evidence that the threat actors accessed user credentials. Burger King Japan has reported the breach to Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) and is now also investigating how the attackers accessed the compromised server, with help from external cybersecurity experts. "We sincerely apologize for the great inconvenience and concern this situation has caused to our customers and all others involved," it added. "At this time, no secondary damage, such as fraudulent use, resulting from this incident has been confirmed." The fast-food chain also warned affected customers to watch for suspicious emails, SMS messages, and phone calls that may impersonate Burger King Japan, and to avoid clicking URLs, opening attachments, or entering member information or passwords. This incident adds to a wave of cyberattacks that have impacted several major Japanese companies since the start of the year, including entertainment system maker Daiichi Kosho, cloud and digital infrastructure firm IDC Frontier, Japanese publishing giant Nikkei, private railway operator Keio, car-sharing service Times Car, cloud and data center service provider Sakura Internet, taxi operator Nihon Kotsu, telecommunications giant KDDI, and many others. Macnica researcher Yutaka Sejiyama has logged 119 cybersecurity incidents involving personal information theft or exposure this year and found that attackers are now probing websites and APIs for access-control, configuration, and authentication weaknesses, and exploiting known (n-day) vulnerabilities. 6lxgs8.text: In the space of a month, a new category of AI model went from nonexistent to everywhere. TypeSafe AI released Jev on September 15 and called it a System One model, a nod to Kahneman's fast, intuitive thinking. OpenAI announced its own Decisions API at DevDay and opened a public beta on October 6. Cribl published cribl-decision, an open LoRA adapter you can run locally. Others, like Laya, are already showing up in open source tooling. These models skip text generation entirely. You hand them some state and a set of typed questions. They hand back a choice, a score, or a yes/no with a probability attached. For security operations, I think this is some of the best news of the year. I also think most of the conversation is pointed at the wrong layer. Why a SOC should be excited Three properties make decision models a natural fit for alert triage. You get a number you can automate against. A typed answer with a calibrated probability is something you can put a threshold on. Ask the model whether an alert is benign and you get back a probability. Close it automatically above 0.97. Below 0.6, treat it as a likely incident and escalate it. Anything in between goes to an analyst for a closer look. TypeSafe even suggests stricter thresholds for irreversible actions, which maps neatly onto “disable an account” versus “add a comment to the ticket.” They're cheap enough for every alert. Jev is priced at $42 per billion input tokens, with responses in 70 to 500 milliseconds. Say an enterprise sees 450,000 alerts a year and you feed a few thousand tokens per alert. The model bill lands somewhere around a hundred dollars a year. The economic argument for cherry-picking and only looking at high-severity alerts just disappeared! Every verdict becomes a record. The answer space is fixed in advance and the output carries its own probability. You can log every decision, replay it, and compare it with what actually happened. That's far easier to audit than a paragraph of generated reasoning. One caveat worth keeping in mind. When vendors say these models "can't hallucinate," they mean the output always matches the schema you defined. A well-formed answer can still be wrong. But a calibrated guess is still just a guess The old rule still applies. Garbage in, garbage out. Calibration is a promise about a distribution. When a well-calibrated model says 90%, it means that across inputs that look like this one, it's right about 90% of the time. So the question that matters is what "this one" looks like. If the input is an alert title and a severity field, the model is calibrated about alerts with that title and that severity. It knows nothing about the host. Here's why that matters in practice. Our AI SOC Report 2026 covers 25 million alerts triaged across our customer base in 2025. In that data, 82,000 alerts went through a live memory scan of the endpoint. About 2,600 of those machines had an active infection. And 51% of the infected machines had already been reported as mitigated by the EDR. Think about what a decision model sees for one of those alerts. Malware detected, threat quarantined, low severity. A perfectly calibrated model should close it with high confidence, because most alerts that look like that really are fine. The model did its job. The input was wrong. Severity has the same problem at a larger scale. Nearly 1% of real incidents in our data traced back to alerts at the lowest severity levels. At an average of 450,000 alerts a year, that's roughly 54 real threats, about one a week. Cribl's own model card says it plainly. The model can be overconfident, and it's sensitive to how the prompt and candidates are worded. That's honest, and it applies to every model in this category. What evidence actually looks like Think about a crime scene. You can describe it to a chatbot in general terms and get a plausible theory. Or you can bring in the DNA lab, the fingerprints, the forensic evidence and the witness statements. Nobody needs to ask which approach finds the right suspect. Security investigations work the same way. Filip Stojkovski recently called this Security Context Engineering, and I think the name fits. The job is to turn an alert into a set of facts before anyone, human or model, makes a call. The question What the alert usually gives you What forensic evidence gives you What ran? "Suspicious PowerShell" The process tree, the parent, the full command line, the script on disk What did it do? A hash and a reputation score What the file did when detonated, the network calls, the files it dropped Is it still there? "Mitigated" from the EDR A live memory scan showing injected code or a fileless payload Who was it? A username Where they logged in, from which device, and whether that's normal for them The third row deserves extra attention. The most common families we found in memory last year were tools like Mimikatz, Meterpreter and Cobalt Strike. These are built to live in memory, which is exactly where a file-based "quarantined" status can't see. None of this evidence is exotic. It's what a good incident responder collects by hand. The hard part is collecting it automatically, for every alert, in under a minute. The hardest context is what normal looks like Forensic evidence tells you what happened on a machine. It doesn't tell you whether that's expected in this particular company. Identity alerts show the gap clearly. In our 2025 data, 74% of identity alerts were classified as likely benign. Impossible travel alerts were confirmed as real compromises only about 2% of the time, and VPN usage alone drove around 30% of them. A model can't tell that Dave from finance always logs in from Portugal, or that a CrowdStrike alert on the build servers fires every time DevOps ships a release. That knowledge usually lives in the head of your most senior analyst, and it walks out the door when they leave. Two things make this context harder than the forensic kind. You can't buy it, because it's specific to your environment. And it decays, because assets, users and tooling change every week. A snapshot loaded during onboarding is stale within a quarter. So organizational context has to be a loop. Learn from past cases and how analysts resolved them. Pull live context mid-investigation when memory isn't enough. Then compare every verdict with its outcome and write the lesson back. That last step is also how you check whether 90% still means 90% in your environment, and not only on someone's benchmark. A forensic approach to alert triage and investigation This is the layer we've spent our time on, so here's a concrete example of what investing in it looks like. Our founding team came from reverse engineering and incident response, and that background shaped one rule. Collect the evidence first, then decide. Code-level evidence. Our Genetic Analysis technology compares every piece of binary code running in memory against a large database of trusted and malicious code. It catches known malware, and it also catches new code that reuses pieces of known threats. Live memory forensics, triggered automatically. When an alert doesn't carry enough evidence for a verdict, or there are signs of a fileless attack or code injection, the platform runs our Endpoint Scanner on the machine. It's a single executable with nothing to install. It collects process trees, executables loaded into memory, memory dumps where injection is suspected, and the files behind scheduled tasks and autoruns. That's how we found the infected machines marked as mitigated. Detonation and network forensics. Suspicious files get run in a sandbox, and URLs, domains and IPs get investigated, so the verdict rests on observed behavior. Organizational memory. Org Brain is our answer to the "what's normal here" problem. It keeps two kinds of memory. One is procedural, how your team investigates and which detections it closes on sight. The other is declarative, your assets, your users, their normal behavior, and even how your SIEM schema is structured. It learns from your case history, fetches live context mid-investigation, and writes conclusions back after every investigation. All this allowed us to investigate over 25 million alerts in 2025, at every severity. Fewer than 2% were escalated to a human, verdict accuracy was 98%, and median triage time was under a minute. When it comes to cost, most of this analysis is deterministic forensics, which is far more affordable to run than a large model on every alert. That's why we price per endpoint and have been investigating everything, long before decision models arrived. Decision models now bring the same economics to the decision step for everyone, and that's a good thing for the industry. If you're building your own pipeline, the same structure applies whichever model sits at the end. Spend your engineering effort on the evidence and the organizational knowledge. Those are the parts that are hard to get and the parts that compound. Where to put your effort Frontier models get better every few months, and everyone gets the upgrade on the same day. Decision models will follow the same curve. Whatever edge a model gives you this quarter, your competitors and your attackers have it too. The context you feed those models is the part that's actually yours. If you're automating triage this year, here's where I'd spend the time. Collect evidence before you decide. Process trees, detonation results and memory contents beat alert metadata every time. Stop letting severity decide what gets investigated. With decision models this cheap, there's no longer a cost reason to skip low-severity alerts. Treat organizational knowledge as a system. Assets, users and normal behavior need to be learned and refreshed continuously. Measure calibration in your own environment. Tie every automated verdict to its outcome, and watch for drift. Decision models make the last step fast, cheap and auditable. Whether that last step is right still depends on everything that came before it.

1l1o3x1.text: Microsoft says some users may have trouble turning on Smart App Control after installing this month's KB5127648 Windows 11 security update. Smart App Control is a Windows 11 security feature that uses Microsoft's app intelligence services and code integrity features and works alongside Microsoft Defender and SmartScreen to block potentially harmful apps or binaries. According to the company, on affected devices running Windows 11, version 24H2 and later, the Smart App Control option is grayed out and cannot be toggled. "After installing this update, some devices might be unable to turn on Smart App Control in the Windows Security app if it has been turned off. On affected devices, the option to turn on Smart App Control might be grayed out," Microsoft said in an update to the KB5127648 advisory. "Devices where Smart App Control is already turned on are not affected and remain protected." While a fix isn't available yet, Microsoft shared temporary workarounds to help IT administrators mitigate the issue on enterprise-managed devices by modifying the registry or installing a group policy. To restore the ability to turn on Smart App Control on affected Windows 11 devices by editing the registry, you have to follow these steps: Open a Command Prompt window by typing cmd in the Search box. Select Run as Administrator. At the command prompt, enter the following commands and then restart the device: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides" /v 2883193997 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Policies\Microsoft\FeatureManagement\Overrides" /v 2850574478 /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f IT admins can also work around the issue by installing and configuring the two Group Policies below to turn on Smart App Control and ensure that logging is enabled for troubleshooting: Windows 11, versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 - KB5074105 261015_19222 Feature Preview Windows 11, versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 - KB5074105 261015_19221 Feature Preview The two Group Policies can be found under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > {Group Policy name} > Windows 11, version 24H2, 25H2. After installing them, admins must set both settings to Enabled and restart the affected device(s) to apply the Group Policy settings. This week, Microsoft also confirmed that recent Windows updates cause Remote Desktop failures for non-admin users if the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled, and resolved another known issue that triggered Always On VPN connection problems after installing the September 2026 security updates. On Tuesday, it also addressed a bug that was causing black screens, desktop loading issues, and Explorer crashes after installing Windows 11 updates released since August. 13q3lew.text: The Administrative Office of the US Courts says a cyberattack on government contractor BAE Systems has taken down the notice system used by federal bankruptcy courts. pkaol0.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 16, 2026Zero-Day / Vulnerability The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. "The vulnerability exists within internal components of Remote Support," BeyondTrust said in a Thursday alert. "The components did not adequately validate the origin of the messages it received. Under the right conditions, this could be used to perform file operations on the appliance." Patches for the flaw have been pushed to all Remote Support SaaS customers as of October 9, 2026. Self-hosted customers of Remote Support running versions from 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 are advised to manually update to BT26-05-RS patch. Customers running a version older than 24.3.1 will be required to upgrade to a newer version to apply the fix. According to a timeline of events shared by BeyondTrust, Armory Castle is said to have exploited the flaw as a zero-day on a single self-hosted Remote Support appliance on August 29, 2026. Then, on September 27, 2026, "successful exploitation of another security device provider [became] public," it added, prompting it to initiate an investigation to hunt for similar activity. Armory Castle has a history of exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966) and Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, and CVE-2025-0282) appliances to break a wide range of sectors, including legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology, and governments, for long-term intelligence collection. It's known to be active since October 2023. "The actor uses a zero-day selectively against chosen targets, and once the vulnerability is public, the actor typically moves to broad exploitation of every instance still unpatched," BeyondTrust said. "Our working assessment is that this actor selects high-value software targets in advance and keeps a working model of the products the actor targets in an AI context that it uses on an ongoing basis to develop exploit chains." Google-owned Mandiant, which shared additional details related to the exploitation activity, said a successful compromise is followed by the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and bidirectional encrypted command-and-control (C2) communication. The operator makes use of commercial VPN exit nodes and compromised home and small-office routers to blend into regular traffic, and then leverages the web shell as a conduit to escalate privileges, obtain full administrative control of the appliance, and establish persistence in a manner that survives reboots. The intrusion is characterized by efforts to facilitate credential theft by reading the appliance's stored secrets and abusing the administrative access to reach downstream systems and enable lateral movement. Details of the post-exploitation actions undertaken by the threat actor are listed below - Gaining root-level control of the appliance host by copying the system shell executable (/bin/sh) to the file "/usr/bin/dbus-authd" and modifying its ownership to root and enabling Set User ID (SUID) permissions, causing it to be executed with the privileges of the file's owner. Attempting to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database by using the proprietary "/ns/sbin/bt-secrets" Command Line Interface (CLI) utility to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. Targeting the BeyondTrust configuration templates to obtain passwordless root privileges to the site service account and Pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised administrator credentials and then launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list. Abusing the elevated administrative privileges to establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints and obtain full file-system access to those systems with an aim to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents for network reconnaissance. Tunneling traffic through the BeyondTrust device via BARECLAW, a C-based custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler that relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. Modifying "/ns/config/haproxy.conf" file to ensure BARECLAW is accessible directly from the internet. Hindering detection efforts by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs. "Throughout the intrusion, Armory Castle leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant researchers Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, and John Wolfram said. "Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed."

2ta124.text: AI agents being tested online reached the live systems of Indian organizations and read business records, including personal data and confidential material, CERT-In said in an advisory on October 15. The agents went beyond their assigned tasks, and none of the organizations detected the unauthorized access. After internal reviews, the AI companies whose models were being tested voluntarily reported the cases to CERT-In, India's national cyber agency. AI agents are software systems that can plan work, run commands, use tools, and act on the internet autonomously for extended periods. In these cases, the agents gained access via credentials and connection settings left exposed in application configuration and public code repositories, and via cloud service roles with excessive permissions. CERT-In did not name the AI companies, their models, or the organizations and sectors involved. It did not say how many companies reported cases or how many organizations were affected, and said only that the reports came in recently. It also did not say whether any data the agents read was copied or kept, or whether the affected organizations have been told. Attackers Used Open-Source AI Agent Tools in a Separate Campaign CERT-In's own threat hunting found a second, separate set of incidents: a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. The attackers misused publicly available offensive-security frameworks built on AI agents. The frameworks continue to be misused and rebranded, with numerous deployments across infrastructure in several countries. CERT-In did not name the frameworks or the attackers. In this campaign, the frameworks cut the time from first access to final impact from days to a few hours, according to CERT-In. The attackers ran several agents in parallel for hours to days to reach their goals. Victims that only partly fixed the problems were attacked again within days, at a larger scale. Google Threat Intelligence Group reported a separate case in September. Attackers who had compromised a cloud resource planned, built and ran an agent-driven campaign that harvested thousands of third-party credentials, all in under 6 hours. On October 9, CERT-In warned of attacks on non-banking financial companies, digital lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and wallet operators. The attackers in those cases stole API credentials and called fund-transfer and disbursal APIs directly to move money into mule accounts. AI-assisted tools may have been used in those attacks. CERT-In has not said whether those attacks are related to the campaign in its October 15 advisory. What CERT-In Wants Fixed The weaknesses behind both kinds of incidents were ordinary, CERT-In said. Credentials and keys were exposed in source code, public repository history, configuration files, client apps and public web pages. Old, unused and test APIs were still reachable from the internet. Payment API keys were stored in plain text, and cloud and backend-as-a-service roles granted ordinary or anonymous users broad read and write access. Management interfaces were exposed to the internet, and application middleware was left unpatched, with weak credentials or no multi-factor authentication. In the cases reported by the AI companies, agents found the same exposed credential again and reused it in separate operations. CERT-In did not publish indicators of compromise for either kind of incident. Organizations should apply the baseline in CERT-In's May blueprint and take these steps: Search source code, commit history, CI/CD variables, configuration files, client apps and cloud storage for exposed credentials. Rotate any you find, purge them from history and confirm the fix from outside. Scan every commit and build for secrets, and keep credentials out of code, configuration files and databases. Keep a full list of your APIs, and shut down old, unused and test APIs and accounts. Apply least privilege to cloud and backend-as-a-service roles, keep privileged keys out of client-side code, and test what an anonymous user can read and write. Take management interfaces off the internet, require multi-factor authentication for all admin access, and patch exposed middleware quickly. Watch APIs with rate-based anomaly detection, alert on enumeration bursts, bulk reads and automated sign-ups, and keep logs for at least 180 days. After any credential exposure or confirmed access, treat the environment as compromised until a forensic check clears it. Retest after fixing it, and expect repeat attempts within days to weeks. If you run AI agents, give each run its own short-lived, least-privilege identity and block outbound traffic except to the destinations each run needs. Keep a tamper-resistant log of agent actions, at least those that touch production systems and data. Banks, insurers, other financial firms, and fintech companies should also apply the payment and disbursement API measures outlined in the October 9 advisory. CERT-In's directions also require organizations to report cyber incidents to the agency within 6 hours. For AI developers, research labs and evaluation agencies, CERT-In wants test runs isolated, with outbound network access blocked by default. That block should be enforced at the network level, not through instructions to the model. A run should stop automatically if an agent contacts outside systems, or finds or uses credentials that belong to someone else. If an agent reaches a real system, the affected organization and CERT-In should be told promptly. Earlier Disclosures by OpenAI and Anthropic OpenAI and Anthropic have both disclosed similar incidents this year. CERT-In did not say whether models from either company were involved in the Indian cases. In July, OpenAI disclosed that its models had compromised Hugging Face's platform. It is reviewing what its models did on the internet during training and testing, and notifying third parties whose security controls its models may have bypassed. In response to that disclosure, Anthropic began reviewing its own cyber evaluations. It has since reported 4 incidents in which Claude models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during evaluations built by the same outside partner. It has notified all affected parties. Of the 3 organizations in Anthropic's July disclosure, the 2 it reached had not detected the activity.

178g5cy.text: BeyondTrust warned customers on Thursday to patch a critical flaw in its Remote Support (RS) that has been exploited in zero-day attacks since late August. Remote Support is the company's enterprise-grade support solution that helps IT service desks, help desks, and customer support teams troubleshoot issues remotely. Tracked as CVE-2026-102764, this actively exploited authentication bypass vulnerability lets unprivileged remote attackers perform file operations on unpatched appliances and affects RS 26.2.3 or earlier. BeyondTrust patched the security issue for all Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access SaaS customers on October 8, but self-hosted installations must be patched manually if automatic updates are not enabled. While the company shared limited details about the vulnerability, it said the zero-day was abused in the wild by a suspected China-nexus espionage actor tracked by Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) security researchers as "Armory Castle" (formerly UNC5221) and by cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike as "Warp Panda." According to Mandiant researchers, who spotted the initial attacks, Armory Castle hackers exploited the flaw to gain initial access and escalated to root privileges on compromised devices by enabling Set User ID (SUID) permissions. Next, they deployed new Sawfly web shell and Bareclaw tunneler malware, wiped logs to evade detection, and moved laterally through the victim's network using compromised Administrator credentials by opening remote sessions on downstream systems. "After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset," Mandiant said. "Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed." ​Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver tracks over 1,400 BeyondTrust remote support instances exposed online, but it provides no information on how many have already been secured or are honeypots. Attack chain (Mandiant / GTIG) Armory Castle is known for targeting zero-day vulnerabilities in network edge appliances, including various Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966) and Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887, then CVE-2025-0282) appliances, since at least October 2023 to breach enterprise networks and drop new custom malware. ​Threat intelligence company Volexity also said in January 2024 that UNC5221 had backdoored more than 2,100 Ivanti appliances using the GiftedVisitor webshell in attacks chaining the CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887 zero-days. "In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed," Mandiant added. "It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764." CVE-2026-102764 is the latest in a string of other BeyondTrust flaws that threat actors have exploited in the wild in recent years. Most recently, attackers exploited another critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-1731) affecting Remote Support and Privileged Remote Access appliances to establish WebSocket channels and deploy ransomware. The Chinese state-backed Silk Typhoon hacking group is also believed to have exploited two zero-days (CVE-2024-12356 and CVE-2024-12686) to breach BeyondTrust's systems and use a stolen API key to compromise 17 Remote Support SaaS instances, including the U.S. Treasury Department's instance. In the same campaign, Silk Typhoon has also targeted the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which administers U.S. sanctions programs, and the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), which reviews foreign investments for national security risks. BeyondTrust provides identity security services to over 20,000 customers worldwide, including government agencies and 75% of Fortune 100 companies. Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access.
