sgo2xe.text: A suspected advanced threat actor has been observed exploiting a security flaw in Fortinet FortiOS to deliver a previously unreported memory-resident ARM64 malware known as PEERSTITCH. The attack involves the exploitation of CVE-2025-61624 (CVSS score: 5.4), a path traversal flaw in the command line interpreter of FortiOS, FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager that could allow a privileged attacker to achieve arbitrary write or delete files via specifically crafted arguments to existing commands. It was patched by Fortinet in April 2026. "PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 researchers Daniel Gott and Shawn Westfall said. "Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection." The cybersecurity company said it discovered the activity as part of its prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider that took place in September 2024. The multi-stage network intrusion is being tracked as CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820), with initial access obtained by exploiting a critical Fortinet FortiManager flaw dubbed FortiJump (CVE-2024-47575). Following a successful compromise of the appliance, the attackers are said to have exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material, and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Some of the harvested details are listed below - The FortiManager appliance's own serial number and its management relationships to every enrolled device Running configuration files for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls across internal infrastructure and client networks Central management SQLite databases An inventory listing more than 500 FortiGate serial numbers alongside their respective public IP addresses Internal network topology maps, routing tables and interface configurations Ciphertext administrative, local, and SSL/VPN credentials Encoded cryptographic trust material, including public certificates, and private keys The stolen information was then used to conduct network reconnaissance, establish long-term access, intercept network traffic, set up unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls, deploy backdoors, and exploit a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability (i.e., CVE-2025-61624) to deploy PEERSTITCH. The malware is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C. It includes an auto-script designed to download five components from an external server ("23.240.77[.]233:8085") - pM.js, an environment preparation script (self-deleting) a.js (saved as index.js), an Emscripten JavaScript runtime module a.wasm (saved as index.wasm), a compiled WebAssembly binary module b.js (saved as ipssem.js), a deployment orchestrator script dd (saved as lldprx), a native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core) The main phase of the attack begins after an execution delay. The orchestrator ("ipssem.js") launches "lldprx," which then serves as a process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons: "/bin/miglogd" and "/bin/iked." Specifically, it locates the running processes associated with the two daemons, enumerates their memory layout, attaches to them using ptrace and halts their execution using PTRACE_INTERRUPT, allocates executable memory and writes malicious code into it, and redirects execution through the injected code. The end goal behind this hooking step is to create a "covert, memory-resident communication bridge" between the two legitimate FortiOS processes instead of using a conventional network connection or file, and use them as a cover to sidestep detection. Specifically, the miglogd hook is equipped to recognize a marker in the data it is passing through the process. This includes two specific markers - TCP port marker - 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port) IP address marker - 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching) Once this pattern is identified, it passes the associated session token or identifier to the iked daemon, whose hook later looks for that identifier while handling subsequent VPN sessions. If such a tag exists within that VPN session's injection buffer, it takes an alternative execution path, bypassing default FortiOS security validations. Put differently, the hooks injected into the two FortiOS processes change how the VPN daemon handles particular sessions. Besides deploying PEERSTITCH, the attackers have been observed establishing a separate command-and-control (C2) channel by leveraging the native Apache "mod_md" module on FortiGate firewalls in order to spawn an SSH-based reverse shell. "The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network," the researchers said. "The attackers demonstrated proficiency in Fortinet appliance architecture, FortiOS internals and FortiOS management protocols." Although not definitive, it's suspected that the attackers may have exploited other flaws like CVE-2024-26009 and CVE-2024-26008 to carry out this task. However, Unit 42 emphasized that exploiting these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, which none of the affected firewalls held. In addition, CL-STA-0954 has been identified as undertaking various measures to remove forensic artifacts through termination of syslog generation, crash log clearing, logging telemetry disruption, and automatic deletion of rogue administrator accounts and auto-script objects after execution. "This intrusion highlights a growing threat, the weaponization of centralized edge management ecosystems to compromise downstream networks," Unit 42 said. "The discovery of the PEERSTITCH implant demonstrates the increasing technical maturity of edge-device malware." "By operating as a one-shot injector, avoiding persistent disk artifacts and building a covert inter-process communication bridge inside process memory, the attackers achieved sustained persistence while evading traditional monitoring."

wlcrsj.text: A cyberattack on a U.S. government contractor has impacted the platform used by all federal bankruptcy courts across the country. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts published a statement on Thursday afternoon warning that a cyberattack on British multinational BAE Systems disrupted the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) — a system that produces and transmits bankruptcy notices for all federal bankruptcy courts. “The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts has been in communication with the impacted courts and is also coordinating with BAE Systems. BAE is actively investigating this incident and working to restore operations,” officials said. “As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service.” The incident has halted all production of bankruptcy notices as well. The office did not respond to requests for further details about the nature of the incident or whether data was stolen. BAE Systems is one of the largest defense contractors in the world and is deeply embedded in the U.S. Government — providing aerospace, weapons and information security services across several federal departments. A spokesperson for the company said they are “aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it.” “We are coordinating closely with [the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts] on the response,” they added. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which typically handles cyberattacks on federal agencies, directed Recorded Future News to the U.S. Courts. The FBI did not respond to requests for comment. The attack on the bankruptcy court system comes weeks after Arizona’s state court system was breached and the information of more than 1.3 million people was leaked. Last year, U.S. federal court officials said they were working to bolster online security for sensitive documents and other case files in an attempt to block cyberattacks and data breaches. The move followed a major hack of the courts’ case filing system which officials feared exposed the identities of confidential informants in criminal cases. The federal courts docketing system was also attacked by hackers in early 2020. The U.S. government has been battered by cyberattacks in recent weeks, with incidents involving the Defense Department and the FBI. On Wednesday, the Department of Transportation confirmed that a safety agency contact center was temporarily taken offline after a contractor was hit with a cyberattack. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

mzuxz3.text: Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-110447, in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud. Multiple administrator reports indicate that attacks began in mid-September, roughly a month before the formal security bulletin, the GitHub advisory, and CVE publication. CVE-2026-110447 impacts richdocumentscode versions before 26.4.303 and resides in the Nextcloud app’s mechanism for starting the bundled Collabora server. The flaw affects only the optional built-in CODE server app. Standalone Collabora Online servers, Docker and RPM/DEB installations, and Nextcloud All-in-One deployments remain unaffected, according to Collabora. The attacks involve sending a malicious request to the app’s proxy.php endpoint, triggering OS command injection. A key prerequisite for successful exploitation is that the built-in CODE server must be stopped (e.g., after a restart, upgrade, crash). Authentication or user interaction is not required. System administrators impacted by malicious activity reported attacks against multiple endpoints dating back to September 10. According to the reports, the attacker planted PHP webshells and used them to search for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets. Some users also reported that ransomware operators are exploiting the flaw, but BleepingComputer could not independently confirm this. System administrators are recommended to upgrade to version 26.4.303 or later, or remove the server app if not needed. The vendor warned that disabling the app is insufficient. Beyond the mid-September warnings from maintainers, a community warning was also published on October 3, urging administrators to update immediately due to ongoing exploitation. However, the lack of a CVE ID made it more difficult for administrators to pinpoint the issue correctly and implement efficient defenses. A study from cybersecurity company Second Security illustrates the gap between security fixes and formal vulnerability notifications. The firm analyzed real-world examples from open-source flaws and found that the median interval between public fixes and CVE publication was 39 days in August, up from 5.1 days in January. The researchers suggest that growing volumes of AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries are straining CVE processing and contributing to publication delays. Source: Second Security In many cases, the researchers found public exploit code emerged online within hours of a security fix and several days before the corresponding CVE was published. Second Security notes that the use of AI tools makes it easy for attackers to generate working exploits for published fixes. Examples of public exploits and CVE appearance timesSource: Second Security In Collabora’s case, the fix was committed on September 9, and version 26.4.303 was released on September 11. The advisory and CVE were published on October 14, a gap of more than four weeks. BleepingComputer contacted Nextcloud with questions about its response to the malicious activity reports, as well as details about the attacks and the number of impacted systems. Nextcloud told BleepingComputer that Collabora reported the vulnerability in mid-September and that an update became available through the app store. The company justified the disclosure delay by saying it gave users time to update and that it had not observed widespread exploitation. In a blog post earlier today about the activity, Collabora attributed the delayed announcement primarily to GitHub CVE-processing backlogs, which it said were under strain from increasing volumes of AI-driven security reports. 16st4el.text: A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed it. The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and nicknamed PwnEscape, is in the Linux kernel's networking code, not in any one cloud's setup, so it reaches the shared layer that cloud providers use to keep customers' workloads apart. It was found in a Vercel security challenge and reported privately before any public release, and there is no sign it has been used in a real attack. What the Researcher Showed Paulos Yibelo of the security firm pwn.ai found that specially made network packets sent from inside a virtual machine could do three things, he explained in a technical write-up: read the host's memory, crash the host, and run code on it. All three come from the same kernel flaw. Vercel said in its report on the challenge that the memory leak was demonstrated against its production sandboxes. Each packet the guest sent out could carry back about 32 bytes of the host's memory, and the guest could keep going as long as it kept sending packets. The crash and code execution were observed only on the researcher's own machines, which were set up to match Vercel's. Two specially crafted packets were enough to crash a host and take down every sandbox running on it. Using the same flaw, the researcher then reached administrator control of a host, breaking out of the virtual machine. He stressed this was a lab result, "not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment." "Our research ran through Omega-Pwn, an internal harness combining our own security research tooling with elements of SingularityNET's OmegaClaw architecture. It let us carry hypotheses, code traces, failed attempts, and experimental results across long-running research sessions. GPT-5.6 Sol was the primary reasoning engine. We directed the investigation, challenged its findings, and validated the interesting ones against actual kernel behavior on systems we controlled," Paulos Yibelo told The Hacker News. Vercel said no report in the challenge showed anyone reading a customer's files, secrets, or application data. How Severe It Is, and Who Can Set It Off The kernel's maintainers assigned the flaw CVE-2026-99999 and, in the published record, rated it 9.3 out of 10, or Critical. The U.S. National Vulnerability Database had received that entry but had not yet finished its own review. The same record lists the attack vector as local. In plain terms, the attacker has to already be running code inside a guest, as the researcher was. This is not a flaw that an outsider can exploit by sending packets across the open internet. It is not in CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, and no real-world use has been reported. Why It Reaches Beyond Vercel Vercel Sandbox runs each customer's code in its own Firecracker microVM, a small virtual machine with its own copy of the Linux kernel, on bare-metal Amazon EC2 hosts. That microVM is the wall between one customer and the host, and between one customer and another. The flaw is not in that wall. It is in the Linux kernel's networking code, which the host runs. pwn.ai said Vercel's sandbox was already hardened beyond normal industry standards, with no misconfiguration it could find. Because almost every large cloud separates customer workloads on the same layer of the Linux kernel, Vercel said that a flaw there poses a risk to shared infrastructure rather than to any one provider. The Fix and the Fixed Versions The fix is a single Linux kernel change, commit 6785011f8b16, written by Red Hat's Michael S. Tsirkin and merged into the mainline kernel. It adds a check that a packet's checksum data cannot point into the IPv4 header before the kernel acts on it, and applies that check at five places in the networking code. The change is deliberately partial. Its author calls it "a defence in depth measure" and notes that a fuller check on the way packets enter the kernel still needs work. The maintainers backported the fix to the stable kernel branches. According to the CVE record, these are the first fixed versions in each supported branch: Stable branch First fixed version 5.10 5.10.272 5.15 5.15.223 6.1 6.1.190 6.6 6.6.159 6.12 6.12.113 6.18 6.18.57 7.2 7.2.11 Linux distributions ship their own kernels and often add this kind of fix without changing the version number, so check your distribution's advisory and whether the fix is in the kernel the host is actually running, not only the number from uname. What to Do Update the host kernel to one of the fixed versions above, or to the vendor build that includes the fix, and reboot into it. Updating only a guest's kernel does not fix the host. The sources give no separate workaround for this flaw if you cannot update yet. Where patching has to wait, the usual step is to limit what a break-in could reach. Vercel said it keeps host kernels up to date, disables nested virtualization, and runs each microVM under Firecracker's jailer, which grants the microVM process only the permissions it needs. That does not fix the flaw, but it narrows what an attacker who used it could do. Found in a $1 Million Challenge The flaw was found in a two-week challenge Vercel ran in August that offered up to $1 million in total to anyone who could break out of its sandbox. No single payout reached that figure. The top reward per report was $50,000; Vercel paid $242,000 across 1,285 reports, and this flaw was the one Critical finding. pwn.ai said it found the flaw in three days using its own AI-assisted research system, with the model doing the source-code analysis and human researchers directing the work. The firm put the cost at under $700 in API tokens. It was the latest case of researchers using a large language model to help find and chain real flaws, after a separate team used one earlier this year to reach internal systems at OpenAI.

6zbabv.text: Google announced new AI-powered defenses against scam messages and call-forwarding abuse on Android, currently rolling out to eligible devices. The new measures aim to address the increased sophistication of scams targeting mobile users, including fraudulent bank alerts and voice-cloning attacks. “Mobile scams have evolved far beyond basic robocalls and phishing texts, turning into sophisticated operations that use spoofed numbers, fake bank alerts, and AI voice cloning,” Google says. “With scams growing harder to spot, it’s nearly impossible for users to catch every red flag themselves,” added the tech giant. Google says its existing Phone and Messages scam detection flags more than 5 million suspected scam calls and texts monthly, but the new measures are expected to catch even more threats. Cloud-based scam analysis The new protections focus on Google Messages and rely on cloud-based Gemini-backed analysis for complex conversations, scrutinizing them for signs of fraud. The system analyzes conversations with unknown senders within the encrypted Private AI Compute environment, protecting user privacy at all times. The new mode also adds on-device Gemini Nano (local AI model) checks for unfamiliar links using real-time web signals, plus clearer warnings before opening links from unsaved numbers. The new cloud-based protections are currently disabled by default, allowing users to activate them. Scam alert on MessagesSource: Google Other improvements Apart from the Google Messages protection, Google has also implemented the enhancements in other areas of the Android system: On-device scam detection in chat notifications, previously launched on Pixel, will reach hundreds of millions more users through Android device partners later this year. Android’s existing sensitive-information masking is now expanding to Chrome and Android WebView, hiding login fields and payment screens during live screen sharing. Android blocks apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warns users before manually entered MMI forwarding codes take effect. Call forwarding warningSource: Google Google is also expanding its verified bank calls system, introduced earlier this year, adding financial institutions from more. This system checks whether a real bank’s call center initiated an incoming call or if it is a spoofing attempt. If the verification fails, the call is automatically ended. Google says that since June it has blocked over 3 million fraudulent calls of this kind for Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone. Revolut and other global financial institutions are also supported. Android users should upgrade to the latest release, keep apps updated, and independently verify caller/sender identities when receiving requests for account-related action or sensitive information. j7vsws.text: Someone built a tool to steal data, then decided it should scare the victim for fun. Yes, that’s an actual feature. And somehow, it fits right in with this week's security stories.The rest gets interesting in different ways. A small permission can lead to a big theft. A trusted login can hide the wrong person. Old bugs are finding new victims, familiar tools are being put to strange uses, and some flaws are so simple you wonder how nobody spotted them sooner.There's a lot more hiding in the details, including a few twists you probably wouldn't expect. Here's what made the list this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. Active ransomware exploitation Qilin and Settra ransomware groups are actively exploiting CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass vulnerability in PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access. The vulnerability, disclosed in May 2026, has since come under active exploitation. "Because this access originates through an organization’s own VPN, malicious activity can resemble legitimate remote work and may go undetected until credential theft, lateral movement, data theft, or ransomware deployment is underway," ReliaQuest said. "Organizations should immediately upgrade affected deployments, disable authentication override cookies where they are not required, terminate all active GlobalProtect sessions after patching, and investigate unexpected connections, including sessions using hostnames such as 'kali.' Patching alone may not remove access established before remediation." Hybrid warfare escalates across Europe Russia is assessed to have escalated its use of hybrid, asymmetric warfare across Europe following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. "They do not involve troops moving across a country’s border or a state’s military dropping bombs on an adversary’s capital city," Recorded Future said. "Instead, they are a complex kit of psychological, cyber, and physical tactics meant to achieve several key aims: (1) Test the enemy’s defensive capabilities, as Russia evaluates whether to escalate aggression into a formal, kinetic conflict, (2) Degrade the enemy’s critical infrastructure, and (3) Sow an environment of fear in the enemy’s government and population to degrade the enemy’s ability to respond." DNS-powered wallet theft Infoblox has analyzed a cryptocurrency wallet-drainer kit, self-branded as Noir, that makes use of DNS TXT records to locate its hosted pool, which currently runs on Cloudflare Pages. It's delivered by means of a loader that queries the TXT record through public DoH services to learn which backend pool is active. "The drainer does not need a seed phrase, password, or private key," Infoblox said. "It tailors content to the user after receiving initial read permissions, developing a plan for the specific wallet. Then it obtains spending permissions that can look less alarming than a direct transfer and performs the theft from attacker-controlled infrastructure." It's suspected that the malware was created and maintained with AI assistance. Discord-based remote access threat A Rust-based remote access trojan dubbed CikaBika Bot has been observed being delivered via a document-themed lure containing a malicious LNK file and a PDF with an embedded payload. "The malware uses a Nim loader, PowerShell UAC bypass, and DLL search-order hijacking before leveraging Discord for C2, reconnaissance, remote execution, and data exfiltration through ngrok in observed malicious activity," Darktrace said. The malware also supports screenshot capture and file transfers. RAT combines theft and intimidation A Windows remote access trojan (RAT) called KGB RAT is being marketed on underground forums since late 2025 as being fully undetectable. It features a built-in crypter, HVNC, credential theft, ransomware, and an unusual set of psychological harassment capabilities, per Group-IB. "KGB RAT is, in practice, a full-featured malware package that gives attackers silent and persistent control over infected Windows machines," it said. "What sets it apart from comparable RAT families is not only its technical breadth — combining credential theft, keylogging, hidden desktop takeover, and ransomware in a single builder — but also a dedicated set of psychological harassment features, including screamer functions, jump scares, and forced blue screens of death. These 'fun settings,' as the developers themselves describe them, signal a threat actor profile comfortable weaponizing victim anxiety alongside data theft." A public disclosure referencing a KGB RAT server at version 0.1 dates to late January 2022, indicating the developer had been building and testing the malware for years before bringing it to market. Stealthy live-screen surveillance A multi-stage infection chain on Windows has been observed deriving a previously undocumented .NET RAT with live screen surveillance capability. It's been codenamed BotHelper RAT. "The first stage is a native x64 stager that fingerprints the host computer name, logged-on user, processor configuration, and installed memory, then connects to easyllms.xyz over HTTPS and retrieves a file named payload.bin from a path guarded by a long hexadecimal identifier, disabling TLS certificate validation beforehand," Point Wild said. "The second stage is BotHelper RAT. It copies itself to a hidden location, registers a scheduled task to relaunch every 30 minutes, patches the Antimalware Scan Interface, and registers with the same host that delivered it before polling a set of PHP endpoints for tasking." New Android anti-scam defenses Google said it's rolling out multi-layered protections across Google Messages and third-party messaging apps to protect Android users against mobile scams. This includes enhanced Scam Detection with Private AI Compute, link safety checks with Gemini Nano, and redesigned warnings before tapping unfamiliar links. Google also said it's bringing Scam Detection in chat notifications to warn users about suspicious messages directly from their notification shade to other Android devices in partnership with device makers. Other security improvements include automatic screen-share privacy to hide sensitive information in native apps, Chrome, and Android WebView, blocking apps from quietly enabling call forwarding in the background, and real-time verification for bank calls in collaboration with Banco do Brasil, Itaú Unibanco, and other leading banks. "Android checks incoming calls in real time to verify whether the bank actually initiated the call," Google said. "If an incoming caller claiming to represent a bank fails this verification check, Android hangs up the call and immediately alerts you." Since launching this feature in June 2026, Android has blocked more than 3 million spoofed calls from Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone. AI model theft defenses strengthened Anthropic has disclosed that new measures like preserved thinking, two-stage classifiers, and charging for requests that are blocked by our safeguards before Claude responds in its Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 models have reduced data harvesting through distillation attacks by about 90% to 99%. Enterprise browser security controls Mozilla has launched Firefox Enterprise, a browser iteration "built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements." Mozilla added, "IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience." Self-healing WordPress backdoor Wordfence has detailed an unusual malware that's installed as a must-use WordPress plugin and makes use of "several self-healing mechanisms in place in order to survive removal. It also makes use of EtherHiding, a technique that hides the location of the attacker's servers behind a smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain, making the command channel resilient to takedown." The malware is capable of establishing administrator access, hiding the rogue administrator account, harvesting administrator passwords, remote site modification, data exfiltration, and spreading to other WordPress installations on the file system. Stolen credentials expose GitHub data Meta said it's notifying about 1,500 people, most of them its own employees in the U.S., after unknown threat actors broke into some of the company's GitHub repositories. The intrusion, detected a few weeks ago, involved the use of an employee's stolen credentials. The access has since been shut down, according to SecurityWeek. XWorm expands surveillance capabilities The malware known as XWorm has transitioned from an infostealer to a full-blown surveillance platform. The malware's plugin count has expanded from 35 to 46. The latest versions detected since July 2025 are V6.4, V6.5 "XWorm Reborn," V7.2, and V7.4. "The Maps plugin provides victims' GPS location without triggering a user prompt," Netskope said. "The Microphone plugin streams live audio from the victim’s device. HBrowser gives operators interactive control of authenticated browser sessions without touching credentials, bypassing MFA entirely. Webcam capture is also available on demand." Higher rewards for memory-safety bugs Google has announced that it's raising bug bounty rewards for some Chrome vulnerabilities, with a focus on memory safety issues. While the company lowered standard payout amounts for some vulnerabilities in April, such as a base reward of $500 for memory safety issues, it has now quadrupled base rates for memory safety flaws to $2,000. Vulnerabilities in Chrome's browser, GPU, and network processes can now earn researchers up to $20,000. Post-quantum readiness warning Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, stating that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. "Organizations should begin now by inventorying certificate dependencies, assessing vendor roadmaps, identifying long-lived infrastructure, and creating non-production test environments," Microsoft said. "Early testing can surface compatibility and process gaps before post-quantum authentication is required at scale." AI tool credentials at risk A new malware-as-a-service (MaaS) infostealer written in Rust comes with its own loader and a built-in cryptocurrency clipper. "Warden Stealer is one of the first infostealers targeting configuration files and local data belonging to AI assistants and agentic coding tools," Gen Digital said. "Its builds are heavily obfuscated, morphed, and regularly updated to evade detection." Advanced browser data theft Newer versions of CastleStealer can "bypass app-bound encryption in Chromium-based browsers, execute commands remotely, and exfiltrate stolen information in small encrypted transmissions rather than a single large archive," according to Flashpoint. The C#-based stealer was first discovered in April 2026. AI developer credentials targeted The infostealer known as Aoki (aka Aokigahara) is targeting credential and session files used by AI coding assistants, including Claude, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor, Codeium, and Gemini. The stealer was first seen earlier this year. "API keys and Open Authorization (OAuth) or session tokens allow malicious activity to be carried out under a legitimate developer's identity and API quota," the Symantec Threat Hunter team said. "They can also expose connected repositories, cloud services and CI/CD pipelines linked to that account, and may bypass safeguards that assume requests originate from a trusted user." In a report published last month, Google-owned Wiz said AI service provider API keys are a hot commodity. "These AI credentials are highly lucrative; allowing attackers to freely run their own workloads or resell the access as part of the illicit LLM resale market," it said. "In addition, these keys can potentially grant access to historical chat logs that may contain sensitive corporate data, but we’re not aware of public occurrences of this scenario." Customizable MaaS infostealer K7 Labs has detailed a Python-based builder that is sold under a MaaS model and is used to embed an infostealer payload. "Rather than operating as a standalone stealer script, the builder follows a MaaS-style model," it said. "It allows operators to generate customized Windows executables using Nuitka or PyInstaller, with webhook configuration integrated into the build process." The stealer capabilities include anti-analysis techniques, persistence, credential harvesting, and data exfiltration. Cloud credential theft risk An SSRF vulnerability (GHSA-2phj-cp9f-qq6w, CVSS score: 8.5) in Harbor, the CNCF open-source container registry, can be abused by a registered user to steal cloud credentials. "Any registered user who can create a project can point a webhook at the cloud metadata endpoint and walk away with the server’s IAM credentials," OX Security said. Unauthenticated RCE chain A set of high-impact vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) can be abused to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). The chain combines four flaws: Unauthenticated DAM bulk import, stored cross-site scripting (XSS), unsafe XML parsing, and Groovy execution via /bin/asynccommand. The flaws affect only the cloud version of AEM and have been patched. Critical unauthenticated RCE Samsung has patched a critical security flaw (CVE-2026-110392, CVSS score: 9.8) in QA-Board that allows unauthenticated RCE. Samsung's QA-Board is an experiment-tracking tool that's used to organize, visualize, compare, and share research runs, specifically for algorithm and performance tuning. The problem stems from a case of improper neutralization of user-controlled data that could result in shell command injection. The vulnerability was flagged by Claude Opus 5.5. Linux root and container escape Security researcher Ziyi Guo has disclosed details of a critical Linux security vulnerability in NVIDIA's GPU Display Driver for Linux (CVE-2026-47595, CVSS score: 7.5, aka Bad UVM) that could allow an unprivileged user can write to read-only memory by taking advantage of the fact that the memory's permissions are not preserved. The vulnerability could be exploited to achieve code execution, escalation of privileges, denial-of-service, information disclosure, data tampering, and even a container escape. "By injecting our exploit code into nvidia-persistenced, we first force the hijacked process to execute a UVM-based local privilege escalation (LPE)," the researcher said. "Once the privilege barrier is crossed, we trigger the subsequent operations, ultimately granting us the ability to execute commands on the host with full root access." Active command injection attacks A command injection vulnerability in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw affects customers using version 2.20 or later with statistics enabled, which is turned on by default. Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary OS commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on affected systems. It's currently not known how the flaw is being exploited, by whom, and who is being targeted. Critical unpatched SQL injection Rapid7 has disclosed details of a critical SQL Injection vulnerability in Channel Software WebAlliance eCommerce (CVE-2026-108065, CVSS score: 9.8). "The exploit allows a malicious actor to read sensitive data from the database, or, if the database user has high privileges, run system commands on the database server," Rapid7 said. "The SQL Injection exploit can be leveraged to view sensitive information in the database, such as user PII and passwords. If logged in with DB admin privileges, the vulnerability can be exploited to run system commands on the server running the database." Four code execution flaws patched NSD has released patches for four security flaws (CVE-2026-101341, CVE-2026-101339, CVE-2026-101338, and CVE-2026-101337) that could be exploited to achieve execution of arbitrary commands. The vulnerabilities, credited to Qifan Zhang from Palo Alto Networks and Gaurang Maheta, have been patched in NSD 4.15.3 or newer. Potential VM-to-host escape The Xen project has published details of CVE-2026-79610, a race condition in Xen's grant-table mechanism that could be abused to compromise the security of a virtual machine host and allow an unprivileged guest to elevate its privileges to that of the host. All Xen versions from 4.0 onwards are vulnerable. The issue has been addressed in xsa517.patch. As mitigation, it's advised to use the "gnttab=max-ver:1" hypervisor command line option or the "max_grant_version=1" guest configuration option for guests. The project maintainers credited Anthropic's Claude Opus with the discovery and Teddy Astie of Vates for diagnosing it as a security issue. SYSTEM-level remote code execution A Windows security vulnerability in MyReport Updater 2.1.1 can permit an attacker to seize control of a machine, including remotely, without authentication. "An attacker with standard user privileges can set an arbitrary reference server," Quarkslab said. "If MyReportUpdaterService can contact this server over gRPC on TCP port 9095, the attacker can write files into a chosen directory with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges. The attacker can use this file-write access to place a DLL that will be loaded by a privileged process. The DLL code is then executed with high privileges. This vulnerability gives full control of the Citrix server. It can also affect other machines where the vulnerable MyReport solution is installed." If there's one thing this week's stories make clear, it's that attackers don't always need a clever trick. Sometimes a stolen login, a forgotten setting, or one small mistake is enough. And even when the bug gets fixed, the trouble it caused might still be sitting there.The lesson is pretty simple: don't just check what's broken. Check who got in, what they touched, and whether they can come back. Keep an eye on the things everyone assumes are safe. Those are often the ones nobody looks at until something goes wrong. That's it for this edition. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

gkosnb.text: A proxyjacking campaign has impacted devices in 34 countries, monetizing victims’ internet connections through a commercial residential proxy network. The operator installed Pawns.app, a legitimate bandwidth-sharing application that lets users earn money by sharing their internet connections, on devices without the owners’ consent. Pawns.app account holders are rewarded for allowing traffic from other users to flow through their network, provided it runs on trusted, non-blocking IP addresses. By installing the app on multiple systems, the attacker likely accumulated larger payouts. Source: GreyNoise Threat intelligence company GreyNoise discovered the campaign while investigating suspicious activity at an unnamed organization, and identified at least 143 compromised devices worldwide. According to the researchers, the attacker leveraged several vulnerabilities to breach edge devices and install the Pawns.app software: CVE-2024-3272 and CVE-2024-3273 in D-Link ShareCenter NAS CVE-2021-44228 in Ubiquiti UniFi Video NVR CVE-2025-31324 in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer The researchers also observed targeting of Hikvision and Dahua DVR/NVR devices, but did not specify the vulnerabilities exploited in these systems. GreyNoise says that, in some cases, the attackers configured SSH key authentication as a backup access method. Configuring SSH accessSource: GreyNoise Even legitimate proxy networks can route suspicious traffic through volunteer-operated nodes due to insufficient oversight, potentially resulting in IP address blocks for participating users or exposing them to allegations of involvement in illegal activities. The FBI previously warned about such networks being used to carry out large-scale credential stuffing attacks against online platforms. GreyNoise provides a free service (account required) for users to check if their IP address is part of a known legitimate or “gray” proxying service. It is generally advisable to avoid downloading software from untrusted sources, as purportedly free software may contain malware that enrolls devices in residential proxy networks. Threat actors also commonly exploit known vulnerabilities in internet-connected devices. Keeping NAS devices, video recorders, and other internet-facing systems updated can significantly reduce the risk of compromise. However, users should also use strong credentials, a secure configuration, and restrict network access. 10ek25h.text: A threat actor uploaded malicious packages to the Arch User Repository (AUR) that impersonated two popular helper tools, yay and paru. AUR is a community-maintained, widely-used package index for Arch Linux and derivative distributions that hosts package build scripts (PKGBUILDs) for third-party and proprietary tools, beta, or older package versions that are no longer available via the official Linux distribution channels. The repository has recently become a target of malicious campaigns, including an attack in June in which 400 packages distributed credential-stealing malware with rootkit capabilities. Another campaign in July prompted Arch to temporarily disable package adoption. The latest campaign was detected on October 13 and involved malicious packages uploaded by a user named “marchos1as” under typosquatted names mimicking the yay and paru command-line tools. Also known as AUR helpers, these tools simplify software management on Arch Linux by streamlining the retrieval and installation of user-contributed packages. A thread on the Arch Linux mailing list named "hundreds of aur packages were mass uploaded with malware" alerted users of the malicious uploads. In minutes, community members confirmed that the packages contained legitimate upstream code combined with a malicious installation script that executed a remote shell script with root privileges. “The package presents itself as a straightforward repackaging of the legitimate 'yay' AUR helper (same upstream URL, same source tarball), but the package name 'yyay' and the malicious install scriptlet reveal it is a trojanised impersonation designed to blend in with the real package,” AUR maintainer Andreas Reichel warned. Another maintainer, Emiliano Gandini Outeda, listed some malicious packages that triggered an alert on his system using rules in his open-source application security tool, TrustSight. The AUR team banned the account belonging to marchos1as and removed the malicious packages from the repository. Reichel says that the payload delivered this way was fetched through a Wayback Machine URL that pointed to a personal repository (hellscripter/install-scripts) hosted on the Russian hosting service GitFlic. Potential links to npm worm A recent report from application security company SafeDep documented an npm campaign dubbed "DirtyBlanket" that fetched code from a ‘hellscripter/install-scripts’ repository on Codeberg. The researchers found a Linux worm that deployed the CHAOS remote-access trojan disguised as a font service, which also injected a loader into AUR packages. Furthermore, an OSV advisory on the "DirtyBlanket" activity describes the same Wayback Machine and GitFlic domain. Despite the connections, there is currently no confirmation that the two operations are related. Arch users who downloaded the suspicious packages should assume that their systems were compromised and take immediate remediation action. 1jd6law.text: Candiru, an Israeli maker of spyware sold to governments, infected devices at the news network Al Jazeera through ordinary online ads, in attacks that needed no click or other action from the user, researchers at the Citizen Lab said Thursday. The hidden attack code ran the moment an ad loaded on the screen, and in some cases the ad loaded out of sight, in the background. The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, said this is the first public, technical confirmation that mercenary spyware, meaning hacking tools sold to governments, has reached real devices through targeted ads. The method had been described before from leaked company documents, but not shown in a live attack. The researchers recovered the spyware itself from one device, but not the exploit that breaks into the browser or app to install it. That first break-in step is described from how the attack was set up, not from captured code. How the Attack Worked The ads were placed by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a normal digital advertising firm. Each ad carried a small piece of code that, when the ad loaded, quietly sent the device's advertising ID and internet address back to a Discover-Tech server, the researchers found. That server decided whether the device belonged to a target. If it did, the server sent back attack code for the browser or app to run. If it did not, the server sent nothing. Because the ad itself carried no attack code, the ad networks that delivered it had nothing harmful to detect. At Al Jazeera, at least 45 devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025, the Citizen Lab said, and it linked the attacks to Candiru with high confidence. The researchers did not say which government was behind the operation. The network gave the researchers its traffic logs. On infected devices, the logs showed the same order each time: first contact with a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru server that screens the device, then a command-and-control server that runs the spyware. Al Jazeera also pulled one Windows program file off a compromised device. Its code used the same distinctive techniques as a Candiru tool the Citizen Lab took apart in 2021, which is the basis for the high-confidence link. Al Jazeera staff were targeted once before. In 2020, dozens of its journalists' iPhones were hacked with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware, in a different operation that used a different method. Who Discover-Tech and Candiru Are Google and the advertising trade group IAB Europe had both listed Discover-Tech as an approved ad vendor from 2020 until this month. The company was registered in Israel in 2020 and is led by its chief executive, Dekel Boni. Candiru is one of the better-known names in the spyware trade. The United States put it on a trade blacklist in 2021 over spyware used to target government officials, journalists, and activists. In 2025, its assets were bought by a U.S. investment firm, Integrity Partners, and moved into a new company, reported to be Integrity Labs, that the sanctions do not cover. What the Platforms Did After the researchers shared their findings, Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their vendor lists in early October, the Citizen Lab said. Google cut off the company's access to its ad exchanges, Beeswax removed it, Vungle paused its access for a review, and Eskimi blocked its accounts. Google told Reuters it had worked with the researchers and removed Discover-Tech "for systematically violating our policies." IAB Europe said it suspended the company after an audit found policy violations. Comcast, which owns Beeswax, said it acted "following recent activity." Discover-Tech, Candiru's owners, Al Jazeera, and the Russian ad network Yandex did not respond to Reuters. Discover-Tech's website was still online on Thursday and said nothing about the findings. How Far the Ads Reached Discover-Tech's reach went far beyond Al Jazeera. On one of its platforms, the company placed nearly four billion ad bids between March and June 2026, the Citizen Lab said, and the ads carrying the hidden callback code appeared in about 75,000 phone apps and 120,000 websites. Confiant, a U.S. ad-security firm that investigated alongside the Citizen Lab, put Discover-Tech's traffic at roughly 10 million ads a day. The ads turned up on the networks of governments and large institutions, the Citizen Lab said, including NATO, the United Nations, European Union bodies, government offices in about two dozen countries, chipmakers, and news organizations. An ad appearing on a network is not proof that anyone there was infected. It shows only how widely the system could reach. Confiant found that the small number of ads it could tie directly to Candiru were low-volume and mostly reached home and mobile internet connections, rather than the sensitive networks themselves. What Defenders Can Check Both groups published the web addresses and files associated with the operation, so defenders can block them and search their own records. Organizations whose staff may have seen the ads, especially on the networks named in the report, can look for the attack's order of connections: a device reaching a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru screening server, then a command-and-control server. Among the published indicators: SHA-256 (recovered spyware sample): 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8 Domain (Discover-Tech ad server): mtrtb[.]com Full list: the indicators in Confiant's report, including the command-and-control servers. Security researchers have warned for years that the ad-buying system could be turned to this use. In December, leaked documents tied the spyware maker Intellexa to a similar ad-based tool called Aladdin, though no live infection through it had been shown.

1sk9stz.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The threat actor known as Silent Lynx has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The activity, observed from June 2025 through August 2026, involves four different infection chains that make use of macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and crafted WinRAR archives exploiting CVE-2025-8088. The attacks lead to the deployment of custom reverse shells like FoalShell, Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell that facilitate interactive remote access to compromised hosts, according to Cisco Talos and Recorded Future Insikt Group, which are tracking the campaign under the monikers UAT-6275 and TAG-193. "UAT-6275's targeting is concentrated in Central Asia, and the wider CIS region," security researcher Ashley Shen said. "Across the reviewed campaigns, observed victims and lure themes span nine countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus." Silent Lynx was first publicly documented by Seqrite Labs in early 2025, highlighting the threat actor's attacks on embassies, lawyers, government-backed banks, and think tanks across Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan. It's assessed to be a Kazakhstan-nexus threat actor active since at least 2020, sharing overlaps with other clusters codenamed YoroTrooper (aka Comrade Saiga, ShadowSilk, and SturgeonPhisher), ShadowSilk, Cavalry Werewolf, and Tomiris. It's suspected that both UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper are part of the same broader activity cluster, although no direct indicator or toolset overlap has been observed between the two. Earlier this year, VMRay disclosed that a threat cluster it tracks as Hydra Saiga compromised at least 34 organizations across 8 countries since December 2024, with reconnaissance efforts extending to over 200 additional targets across the world. It's worth noting that both Comrade Saiga and Hydra Saiga refer to the same threat actor. The "hydra" prefix in the tracking alias is a reference to the adversary's heavy focus on breaching infrastructure linked specifically to water resources in Central Asia using a mix of custom implants written in Rust, Go, and Python and Living-off-the-Land techniques. Attack chains mounted by the threat actor involve the use of spear-phishing emails containing diplomatic relations, international trade, energy, and aviation-themed decoy documents. No less than eight campaigns have been identified across the region between January 2025 and May 2026. The phishing emails are sent from compromised government accounts and make use of official-looking documents to lend the social engineering attack a veneer of credibility. "Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery," Recorded Future said. What's more, three publicly accessible staging directories linked to the threat actor have been found to host Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2025-25257, an SQL injection flaw in Fortinet FortiWeb, suggesting a possible expansion of the threat actor's operational capabilities. Infection sequences have been found to employ four different pathways - June 2025 - Using macro-enabled Word documents to download and run a second-stage binary. July 2025 - Using downloaders built with PS2EXE, a tool that packages PowerShell scripts as Windows executables, to fetch reverse-shell payloads and create scheduled tasks for persistence. October 2025 - Using a malicious shortcut (LNK) within a RAR archive to launch PowerShell responsible for retrieving and executing a GitHub-hosted script that provides remote shell access. Subsequent iterations also download PickleShell and stage it in the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically launched every time a user logs in to the system. April 2026 - Using a RAR archive that exploits a WinRAR flaw (CVE-2025-8088) to drop PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder. The April 2026 infection chain marks the first time UAT-6275 has weaponized a security flaw as part of its malware delivery methods. "UAT-6275's sustained activity and adoption of new delivery techniques suggest the group will continue pursuing access to government organizations across Central Asia and the CIS," Talos said. "Its interest in environmental agencies, economic ministries, and energy infrastructure reflects the intelligence value of regional diplomacy and resource management."

yrpqjw.text: A long-running Traffic Distribution System (TDS) known as Help TDS to a Russian-language affiliate program called Hotejka, which appears to be a rebrand of a traffic monetization operation dubbed ROI777. Help TDS is assessed to be active since at least 2017, offering PHP code templates to partners and affiliates that are installed into compromised websites with an aim to direct unsuspecting users to tech support scams. These scams make use of full-screen browser manipulation and exit prevention techniques to serve bogus Microsoft Windows security alert screens instructing victims to contact a Windows Support number to address the problem. "Help TDS delivers tech support scams (TSSs) that direct users to call centers, where social engineering is used to convince them to install remote desktop tools," Infoblox said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It's not simple credit card fraud: it's remote access, living-off-the-land malware operations. Once in, the threat actor can exploit the victim time and again." Help TDS's evolution was documented by GoDaddy in August 2025, highlighting the threat actor's use of a malicious WordPress plugin named "woocommerce_inputs" on thousands of websites to steal WordPress user credentials and facilitate the malicious redirections by fetching the URLs from its command-and-control (C2) servers. The plugin, or alternatively a custom HTML block, is injected into the sites by Hotejka's affiliates. Historical tracking of malicious redirect chains has also uncovered that Help TDS has routinely handed off traffic directly to VexTrio Viper, a cybercrime operator that runs an affiliate program to enable scams, riskware, spyware, adware, and pornographic content. The latest findings connect the TDS to Hotejka, which, in turn, is suspected to be a successor to ROI777, an entity that was exposed by Guardicore Labs (now part of Akamai) in June 2018 in connection with a traffic manipulation and cryptocurrency mining campaign codenamed Operation Prowli. The activity involved the compromise of vulnerable servers to deploy a malware named r2r2 and then leverage them to mine cryptocurrency. In tandem, WordPress sites and servers running other content management systems (CMS) were exploited for traffic monetization fraud. "Traffic monetizers, such as ROI777, buy traffic from 'website operators' such as the Prowli attackers and redirect it to domains on demand," Guardicore Labs noted at the time. "Website 'operators' earn money per traffic sent through roi777. The destination domains frequently host different scams, such as fake services, malicious browser extensions and more." The rebrand is believed to be driven by the leak of data obtained from ROI777's servers in March 2018, around when it was operating Disposable TDS, a precursor to Help TDS. The published details included Telegram identities of its users and details of multiple campaigns. The connection between Hotejka and ROI77 doesn't end there, for GoDaddy also found that "roi777[.]com" was one of the historical C2 domains used between 2018 and 2020 to fetch the redirect domains. "[Hotejka's] affiliates range from spam operators to website compromisers," Infoblox said. "Potential victims are redirected into the TDS from these affiliates via special URLs provided by Hotejka. The TDS then evaluates the user via browser fingerprinting and location to determine the course of action." A TDS functions akin to a relay, intercepting internet traffic from compromised websites, malicious ads, social media posts, or SEO spam, analyzing the visitor, filter traffic based on predefined criteria (e.g., geographic location, device metadata, IP reputation, and headless browsers), and dynamically route them to scams, browser lockers, or malware drops. "Help TDS and its precursors are the routing decision infrastructure for a small affiliate program," Infoblox explained. "Other threat actors, for example ones who have compromised websites, send potential victim traffic to the TDS through specially crafted URLs." The TDS is believed to be implemented on Keitaro, an advertising performance tracking platform that's known to be abused by various threat actors. Some of the initial Help TDS lures prompt users of an impending Windows update, followed by a warning that the machine has been disabled by Microsoft, tells them not to restart the computer, and that a "computer lock" has been put in place to block illegal activity. The scareware prompt is designed to persuade the victim to contact the Microsoft Technical Support team. Should the victim make the phone call, the threat actor on the other end instructs them to download and install a free remote desktop tool like Ultraviewer to gain complete control of the infected machine. The fingerprinting step determines whether to route the user to either the tech support scam or to another affiliate marketing platform, which then evaluates the device again and resells the traffic. These pathways lead to scam landing pages with fake CAPTCHA checks to enroll the victim's browser to push-notification spam. "Historical DNS records, loyal use of other affiliate advertising platforms over the years, and consistent command-and-control (C2) mechanisms give us a high degree of confidence that ROI777 and Hotejka are one and the same," Infoblox said. Messages posted by Hotejka on their Telegram channel (@hotejka_hot) demonstrate their criminal intent by advertising forced browser extension installations and tech support landing pages that are "very difficult to exit." In one post dated July 17, 2026, the operator claimed a "small call center in Germany will handle 50-100 calls per day." Since April 2026, the scams are run on free Cloudflare Pages sites (*.pages[.]dev), with the threat actor creating roughly 300 disposable pages per day. Over 20,000 such domains have been detected since then. In recent years, Hotejka has also been observed using different aliases on forums like CrackingX, seeking traffic from email spam and access to WordPress admin panels for prices starting at $100. In all, about 20 different affiliates, including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay, send traffic to Help TDS. These operations are known to heavily target WordPress sites to redirect victims to scams and malware. "Hotejka/ROI777 has been loyal to the two affiliate platforms since 2017, and we believe that loyalty has paid handsomely," Infoblox said. "Using DNS volumes observed over the past 8 years, our ability to use affiliate IDs to track traffic over time, and commonly cited payout figures for affiliate advertising in general, we suspect that the two European programs have paid them at least a few million dollars (USD)."

1xcsnze.text: With the rise of AI pentesting, a lot of people are wondering if it’s as good as a human. Having started as a pentester twelve years ago, and having moved through similar roles to working on Intruder’s AI pentester, I've come to understand the advantages and disadvantages of both. Here’s how they compare. The strict methodology was never the good bit You may expect AI pentesters to follow strict methodologies in the way that many human pentests do. At Intruder, we experimented with this approach early on - structured systems where each agent had a specific vulnerability type to look for. What we found was that agents would miss things outside their remit entirely, or miscategorize what they did find as the one thing they'd been told to look for, causing confusing reports. A complete lack of structure also failed to produce good results, as completely free agents without any guidance couldn’t break down and manage large applications properly. They could find interesting things, but at the cost of missing a load of other vulnerabilities in our targets. We’ve put a lot of testing into finding the balance between these approaches, and settled on giving agents freedom with broadly defined roles to help them approach and manage large applications, and stricter guardrails to stop them causing damage. This does mean that our AI pentester doesn’t tick off the parts of a methodology document that you’d typically see in a human pentest. That may make some people uncomfortable - a strict methodology gives people assurance that someone has gone through your application and tested everything on the list. An unauthenticated SQL injection needs to be found, and a checklist is there to make sure it does. The methodology gives a lot of people the idea that a human pentest is a perfectly repeatable product, as any tester will be able to follow the methodology, and everything important will get found. The reality is a lot more nuanced than that though, as pentesting is a skilled job, and many of the most impactful findings on a pentest will come from the tester being experienced in noticing weird behaviours and following up on them. For our AI pentester, we ended up with much more interesting and impactful results by not trying to guide our agents through specific vulnerability types. A good example is a complex authentication bypass the agents found that had been sitting in a codebase through five years of pentests without any human testers picking it up. The mechanics of that issue mean that you’d never think to write a testing guide that could be strictly followed to identify it, and if we’d tried to limit our AI pentester too much it never would have found it either. You could say that only finding the common things would still be pretty good, but there's such an array of vulnerabilities that aren't common that you find during a pentest. And just because they’re not common, it doesn’t mean that an attacker can’t find them too, especially now AI is being used to enable attacks more. A strict methodology being carried out by a competent tester only ever provided a low baseline of reliability, and it didn’t even do that perfectly. What makes a pentest good is the part that a skilled tester does outside the checklist, and that's where AI thrives - following its nose through your application and finding the things that were never going to make a list. What they know, and what they can’t ask Our AI pentests take a white box approach, which means the agents get the source code. They work through the entire codebase and build a picture of not just what every page is, but how the application is meant to function and what requests can be made. Doing this to the level of detail that the AI is able to isn’t feasible for a human pentester during a typical time window for a pentest. The AI pentester also builds up a sense of what the application is for, and a good example of this is access control - it doesn’t need to be told that low privileged users shouldn’t be able to reach admin functionality, or that a particular bit of data is sensitive. You can give them extra information as well, just like a human tester. For example, people often specify that they’re worried about their customers being able to access each others’ data, and the pentester has done a great job of focusing on these issues and identifying a lot of them. What the agents can't do is ask you for anything you didn't already give or tell them. If I don't understand what a part of an application does while I’m doing a pentest, I can ask my contact, and those conversations can be very useful for testing the application properly, and assessing risk in the final report. I can also clarify the scope with my contact if needed, or ask for permission to verify something when I’m unsure if there’s a risk of disruption. We’ve had to deliberately make our AI pentesting agents cautious on this front to avoid going out of scope. Neither finds everything The freedom that lets AI pentesting agents find something like a complex auth bypass is the same thing that makes them less predictable. They decide where to dig, and that won't be identical every time. But pentest results have always varied with the person doing them. It's why many consultancies will rotate your tester each year - different people find different things on the same application. This comes down to people’s experience, specialisms, and incidental knowledge. I’ve found issues because of a blog post or specification I happened to read years earlier and was left sitting in the back of my head. And even the things on a checklist get missed sometimes. People are fallible, and covering an entire application methodically over multiple days can be hard. Consistent coverage is something we're actively working to improve, but it’s not something that was ever offered perfectly from anyone. It's why every human pentest report comes with a disclaimer saying as much, even though most people read it as a formality. The remediation I couldn’t have written Every pentester has strong opinions about what makes a good report. I’ve built up many of my own over the years, as have the rest of the current and former pentesters at Intruder. These opinions are what we built our report around. The executive summary is the hardest page of a report to get right. For a lot of people it's their entire experience of your work, and at a good consultancy a lot of effort goes into it. We’ve worked to get to the point where the agents are now writing genuinely good ones, and I often read them first on our own reports to get a good overview before diving into detail. Where they're still off is scoring risk. They rate things higher than I would, partly because they can't have the conversations with you that would bring a rating down, and partly because LLMs err towards caution when you start talking about cybersecurity. That's the right direction to be wrong in, but it does mean you'll see things flagged as more serious than they are, and it's something we're working on. Remediation guidance is where the agents excel. After a long week on a pentest it's tempting for a human to write generic advice, and you catch yourself and try to do better. Unfortunately, you're usually limited by time and usually by not having the source code. The agents don't have either problem, so they'll tell you the line of code to change, and what to change it to on every issue. They also write about mitigating controls that can help reduce the impact of the issue, or provide a temporary fix. We're seeing that speed up how quickly people actually fix things. We had a customer with 78 issues who fixed all of them within a few days, which as a human pentester I have never seen happen. I couldn't have written the level of detail that made those fixes possible in the time I'd have had. So is AI pentesting as good as a human? AI pentesting and human pentesting are different, and once you stop trying to rank them the comparison gets a lot more useful. The agents are finding serious issues in applications that human testers have already been through multiple times. They'll read a whole codebase, work through every path in it, and write up every instance of what they find with the fix down to the line of code. And you can run one whenever you want. For what a single human engagement costs you can run four AI pentests, which means you can do deep testing on a regular basis rather than once a year. That’s a key thing that is missed by human pentesting, and often applications have undergone a lot of untested changes in between pentests. See what Intruder’s AI pentester finds in your application. Learn more. Author Written by Daniel Thatcher, Security Research Engineer, Intruder Daniel is a security researcher at Intruder with a background in penetration testing, and a focus on exploiting web applications in black-box scenarios. rxlfj4.text: Microsoft announced that Windows Server 2022 has reached the end of mainstream support and will remain in extended support until October 2031. Microsoft unveiled Windows Server 2022 in March 2021 and made it generally available in September 2021 as a Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release with 10 years of support. "As of October 13, 2026, Windows Server 2022 has reached end of mainstream support and transitioned to extended support. The October 2026 security update is the last mainstream support update available for this version," it said. "Extended support includes security updates at no additional cost, and Windows Server 2022 will continue to receive monthly security updates through October 14, 2031." Microsoft has also extended Windows Server 2022 hotpatching until October 2027, one year after the mainstream end date of October 2026, for systems running the Datacenter: Azure Edition. Before Windows Server 2022 reaches the end of support, Microsoft advised IT admins to upgrade to Windows Server 2025, which began rolling out to Windows Insiders in January 2024 and reached general availability in November 2024. "Windows Server 2025 is the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release for Windows Server. To help keep your environment protected and supported, plan your upgrade path to Windows Server 2025 for full mainstream support," the company added. According to Microsoft's lifecycle platform, Windows Server 2025 will reach its end of mainstream support in November 2029, with an additional five years of extended support until November 14, 2034. Those who want to test it before deployment can use the free 180-day Windows Server 2025 trial available via the Microsoft Evaluation Center. You can find more information about Windows servicing dates on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or using the Lifecycle Policy search tool. On Tuesday, Microsoft also announced that devices running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions no longer receive security and non-security preview updates and advised customers to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2 (the latest Windows 11 version, also known as the Windows 11 2026 Update). Last week, it also warned users to upgrade devices running unsupported versions of Windows because they will stop receiving security updates after next year's Windows Update certificate rotation.
